speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday I promised to give an answer to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) regarding outstanding excise stamps which were purchased in connection with the stamp tax on cheques. My colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, informs me that on the day following the budget his department issued instructions to banks and business concerns with an undertaking to redeem unused stamps and embossed cheques. maintopic: BLOOD TESTS BEFORE DELIVERY TO THE UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: BLOOD TESTS BEFORE DELIVERY TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yesterday on the orders of the day the hon. member for Middlesex East asked if instructions had been issued to the government veterinarians not to take blood tests until March 2 of purebred cattle sold for delivery in the United States during the first week in March, and suggested that such instructions would cause delay in delivery and financial loss to the livestock industry. I indicated that I was not aware of any such instructions being issued.
1 have made inquiries and find that under date of February 20 instructions were issued to all district veterinarians that it was expected the embargo against the importation of cattle and livestock products into the United States from Canada would be removed on March 1 next and it would therefore be in order for them to advise all concerned that they would be prepared to inspect and prepare cattle for export to the United States on request, in accordance with the bureau of animal industry regulations in effect prior to February 25, 1952, when the United States department of agriculture prohibited the importation of Canadian livestock and livestock products into that country.
In other words, the instructions were just the opposite to that suggested by the hon. member, and the department had already taken action to see that there would be the minimum of delay in such movement so that there would be no financial loss to the livestock industry.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, February 19, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission and the permission of the house, before I address myself to my task I would like to say a word on behalf of those of us who sit on this side of the house about the late deputy minister of finance. I myself had the good fortune to be associated with him in personal ways because we were members of the same university. In that connection he was full of wisdom and full of the spirit of helpfulness. Since I have been here as a member of parliament I have realized not merely the validity of the praise which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) generously gave him the other night, but also that as regards every member of this house, regardless of where he sat, the late deputy minister of finance was only too anxious to assist so far as he could in the discharge of the duties of any and every one of us.
Now, Mr. Speaker, on Thursday evening last I expressed indignation at the practice apparently growing and becoming accepted whereby tax reductions are mysteriously synchronized with election years. I believe that is all wrong because I think it is a clear indication that tax reductions are timed and gauged not in the interests of the taxpayers and not in the interests of the country but in the interests of the government of the day.
I complained further that tax reductions were not the result of economy but merely rebates of still further exactions which the minister was making from the taxpayer. I complained that it was a kind of cat-and-mouse game where the government every few years is kind to the mouse in the hope of treating him still more scurvily later on.
I complained of extravagance and I gave illustrations of it. I complained that there was precious little in this budget for the small man. I complained particularly about


the extravagance in the Department of National Defence and finally I said, having regard to all the considerations I had brought forward or referred to, that I thought a reasonable person could conclude that if there was a really urgent and insistent attack on the problem of economy and efficiency huge sums might be saved.
Well, Mr. Speaker, as one surveys or reflects upon the budget since Thursday last, when it was presented, one realizes more than ever that we are witnessing a very interesting spectacle. The spectacle is that the government is offering, in return for votes, to give back to the voters a little of the huge amounts it has taken from them. No, Mr. Speaker, I am wrong. The government is not offering to give this rebate to the taxpayers as a whole because, as I say, the great majority get little or no benefit of any kind.
The offer is to give this rebate to a small and select proportion of the taxpayers, and the general body of taxpayers apparently is expected to be so pleased at this relief given to others that they will be full of gratitude to the government. It is a simple and interesting idea, Mr. Speaker, and I shall be very interested indeed to see whether it works out. My belief is that it won't.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have heard that before.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I listened last Thursday to the apparent glee of government supporters, as evidenced by their rapping of desks, I remembered that last year there had been joy on the evening of the budget but on that occasion it was a matter of hours' duration and when we waked in the morning, "behold, it was a dream." The joy had turned to sorrow quickly. Indeed, it was no time before public opinion, as evidenced by the press, began to reproach the minister for what he had done. I will quote briefly from two newspapers, one east and one west. The Hamilton Spectator said:
If Mr. Abbott ever again has to perform the income tax sleight-of-hand he achieved on Tuesday's budget, we suggest that he let us know in advance so we can get in the mood for it.
The Calgary Herald said:
It can be said without fear of contradiction that Mr. Abbott makes most vaudeville magicians look clumsy. His hand is indubitably faster than the eye . . .
May I remind the house that the reason for those sour observations was that after the first joy was over it appeared that the income tax relief then, as now, missed most of the people in the lowest income brackets. After effect was given to the social security rate,

in the first half of 1952, on a taxable income of $1,000, far from there being relief a man had to pay $10 more. A man with a taxable income of $2,000 had to pay $16 more; and it was only when you got higher up the situation was different. A man with an income of $7,000 paid $20 less. This year it looks like a repeat performance, but let us see what it means in terms of actual dollars and cents.
In 1952 there will be no change-we will be making our returns very shortly. The taxpayer this year, as distinct from 1949, must wait for his social dividend until July 1. That was not the case in 1949 when Santa Claus went back to January 1. It does raise the question, perhaps, whether the minister is holding back on us and keeping some sweetening for a later date.
When it comes to 1953 we find, as we did a year ago, that the loaves are for the people with larger incomes and that those with smaller incomes seem to have only crumbs. For instance, if you take into account the social security tax, and we must take it into account, a married man with two dependents and an income of $5,000 is $18 better off. A married man with $3,000 is $4 better off and a man with $2,400 will receive the magnificent relief of $1. An unmarried single taxpayer is in the same class as the $2,400 man-he gets $1.
That raises the interesting question of how many of the taxpayers, how many of the earners, how many of the people who contribute to this result, are in the tax reduction picture. I can give you some figures. In 1951, the last year for which I have figures available, there were 4,950,000 earners. Of those, 2,172,000 paid no income tax, and 1,694,500 of those who paid taxes had incomes of $3,000 or less. The result was that roughly 75 per cent of the earners got practically no benefit from tax relief at all.
So much for the $100 million that was attributed to the personal income tax. We come now to the corporation tax which was reduced $97 million. We have believed, and we have said, that the minister has been mulcting corporations too much. We believe that the result of what he has done has been to drive down corporation earnings in 1952, and the evidence of 1953 is still more discouraging. We are glad that the minister has realized, even after a year, the mistake which he made a year ago. We are all interested in corporations. We are interested in two ways. First of all we are interested that corporations should produce goods at the lowest possible price, and secondly that they may be able to employ 68108-149
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
labour at the best rates. Therefore, if the situation is allowed to continue long enough where corporation earnings are going down, it will be injurious for us all. We can all, therefore, express gratitude that the minister has repented of the evil he has done. The only thing for which we do not forgive him is doing it at all.
As I shall show later, perhaps more than once, Mr. Speaker, we complain that those actions which have been taken, and which we deprecate, are all due to the fact that there is not yet in this government any effective attack on waste and extravagance. So far as the relief to small corporations is concerned, we on this side of the house take credit for that ourselves. We have hammered on that for years, and we will congratulate ourselves, though we will hardly expect the minister to admit that he has at least learned from us.
Now, the remaining $40 million of tax relief comes in odds and ends in certain special excise and sales taxes and in concessions to investment income. Not many of the 75 per cent who get little or no help from the income tax relief, Mr. Speaker, will get very much help from the 20 per cent increase in the amount of deductible dividends. I imagine most of them will find plenty of use for their money in buying food and clothing for the children. I do not think we need assume for one moment that any of them is trudging down to open safety deposit boxes to see his preferred shares or to calculate how much relief he is going to get on his 20 per cent deduction.
There are people however to whom the 20 per cent deduction is quite interesting indeed. Take the case of a married man with two children having no earned income, but having $8,000 of income from share dividends. This is how the matter works out for him. His exemption is $2,300, so he pays a tax on $5,700. His normal tax is y	.anc* his special investment tax is
$224. His total tax, therefore is $1,373.50. But he does not pay it, Mr. Speaker, because
able t0 set off 20 Per cent of the $8,000 or $1,600. His tax is $1,373.50 and his permissible deduction is $1,600, so as a result he pays no income tax at all. That is very nice for him, but I doubt if the government will get very many votes from the fellows below, let us say, $3,000 by reason of their assistance to that man.
Of course, if you smoke enough you may make money out of the budget. If a man smokes a package a day, every day of the year-I understand that is a very moderate amount of smoking-I have calculated that he will make about $15 a year. I hope my

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell arithmetic is good. Of course, he would have to spend $125 to get that. I imagine that most of the fellows earning $2,400 a year, with two children, will be rolling their own or perhaps some of them will be smuggling them. At any rate, I would not think that the amount of money that would be made out of that would be very great.
A moment ago I referred to the loud acclaim, the plaudits of last Thursday, the smiles on every face; but I begin to wonder whether the smiles will turn into smiles _ of irony or disillusionment when the realization gets abroad, as it is getting abroad very rapidly, as to how many taxpayers are left out. I might mention in particular the farmers and fishermen who have been left out. Any benefits to them are picayune. Their only hope of getting any benefit is to be high-income tax payers. Then, of course, the farmers have a special grievance because there has been imposed on them a 15 per cent excise tax on replacement tires and tubes used on trailers, etc. This is all the worse because the farmer is hit at a bad time when many farmers are suffering from a loss of markets. It is just as if the farmer not only got nothing done for him but had to take a slap on the face for his pains.
The other night the minister told us, in summing up the achievements of his budget, that he regarded the relief given as a social dividend. I was surprised at that, and the more I think about it the more surprised I am. I have always thought of a social dividend as a dividend which would apply across the board. When I find benefits which seem to enure largely to a small class, called social dividends, I find that the words are used in a sense that is quite surprising. I cannot overlook the fact or refrain from pointing out that the minister, if the savings had been available, and I shall come to that later, could have done something through the sales tax for those who are left out of this budget. The minister has never been very sympathetic to us in our representations with regard to the sales tax. It seems to me he takes the attitude that the sales tax is not burdensome and he points to the undoubted fact that there are important exemptions from it. He seems to make every effort to make himself believe that it does not bear very hard on the ordinary household. I believe he is quite wrong, because a large number of the ordinary things which every person has to buy are still covered by sales tax.
Now, to sum up, Mr. Speaker, there is no need to elaborate the point further. It is obvious that the great bulk of the relief given by this budget is confined to the few,

let us say to 25 per cent of the population. For the 75 per cent of the population there is little or no relief. They are not in the sunshine, they are in the cold shade. The truth, as I say, is beginning to seep in. I noticed, to my surprise, that on Friday and Saturday there were comments in the press that there was something for everybody. I suppose if you define "something" as microscopic enough that may have been literally true. But it seems to me that it was an entire misreading of the budget, and I think that the truth is coming home very rapidly. For instance, here is an article from the Edmonton Journal of February 20:
For several million Individual Canadian taxpayers, finance minister Abbott's tax concession exposed last night . . . will seem little more than crumbs from a rich man's table.
The Post-Record of Sydney for February 21 said:
Only those too easily dazzled-
May I say with respect that I thought there were a lot of people in this chamber on Thursday night who were too easily dazzled.
-are saying that finance minister Abbott brought down a sunshine budget in the Commons on Thursday night.
There is one short quotation I should like to read from Le Devoir of February 20:
Some $300 million (of the surplus) are gone, but we still have a balanced budget. The prestidigitator has had a perfectly successful pre-electoral performance. It would appear extraordinary if it were new, but we are used to Mr. Abbott's hocus-pocus.
I do not know what that is in French. I shall have to learn later.
People also may have vague memories of 1949. If they go back to 1949, they may discover one or two interesting things with regard to taxation. I put them on the record, and I am sure the gentlemen, particularly those on my right, will be interested. In March, 1949, the government repealed the tax on all soft drinks sold in bottles, but the next year placed on soft drinks a 30 per cent tax, the heaviest in history. In 1949 the minister repealed the 30 per cent tax on candy and confectionery. A year later he raised it again to 30 per cent. In 1949 the minister repealed the 50 cents per pound tax on carbonic acid gas but in 1950 he restored it. In 1949 the government repealed the 30 per cent tax on chewing gum but the next year it was restored at 30 per cent.
What do we on this side of the house say about those reductions? Do we complain about them? On the contrary, Mr. Speaker. When the minister speaks about incentive and the need for encouraging production, the words sound familiar to us. We seem to

remember using words of that kind ourselves. When the minister confessed the injury done to corporations and the need for correcting it, that too is a familiar theme to us. We seem to remember raising this point ourselves. As I said a moment ago, the welfare of so many of us-wage earners and consumers-depends on reasonably profitable operations of corporations. These arguments have been used before, and any sensible man would use them.
Our complaint is that it should have been possible to do these things and other things as well, and that if there was due economy we would not have had to stop there with the 25 per cent but that we could have thought about the 75 per cent. As I say, our complaint is that it was not done before and that it is too little and too late. The minister really admitted a good deal of these things when he said a year ago that the additional corporation tax was unsound. What he should have done, Mr. Speaker, was not to increase that corporation tax which he himself told us was a wrong thing to do but to look around and get the economy which would have enabled him to avoid this tax.
Then there is the removal of the radio licence fee. We have shouted long and loud for that and we approve of it. But we certainly do not approve of the scheme-and an extremely strange scheme it is, it seems to me-whereby the 15 per cent excise tax on television machines is to be earmarked apparently for television services. Those things seem to me to have no relation whatsoever. Why on earth the number of television sets bought should fix the income of the C.B.C. on its television side is something that I cannot understand. It seems to me to be perfect nonsense. Nobody will argue that these things are related and it does not need much courage to predict that that scheme will not last very long.
I have said that our complaint is that these benefits are too narrow, and that they could have been extended if the government would really grapple with the question of the elimination of waste and extravagance. No one is more conscious than I am that those are not new words to use in this house, but I shall try to establish later that we perhaps have a new situation which may make them more effective than they have been in the past. The Minister of Finance no doubt is the prisoner of other departments. At any rate, the assumption of his whole statement the other night-and the assumption made by the government-is that the present spending level is virtually irreducible and that therefore no further tax relief is possible.
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
Mr. Speaker, we repudiate that assumption utterly; and we believe that an increasing number of people share our views. This is a good thing because it is perfectly clear that we are just wasting air in expecting economy until the hand of the government is forced. The Winnipeg Free Press, which I am always glad to quote-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is good old stuff.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sometimes old stuff becomes new. As I say, the Winnipeg Free Press, which I am always glad to quote, on January 30 has an editorial with a brisk little heading. It is entitled "Quick, the Axe". What it wants the axe used for is because of the C.B.C. broadcast to South America of which the Free Press says "No more wanton extravagance could be imagined."
What is needed, of course, is to bring this sort of thing to the consciousness of the ordinary voter and still more to make him believe that something can be done about it. I wish to refer to a little illustration given by a writer recently. He breaks down the federal expenditure of roughly $4J billion. He says that is $375 million a month. He says that, on the magic calculation of averages, that is $25 a month, on the average, for every man, woman and child or $100 for a family of four. He says with force that if you could make the ordinary family believe that they are paying $100 a month in taxation, of which $50 is for defence, they would really sit up and take notice. I think that is true.
In general terms what we say, Mr. Speaker-and I go back now to the words used by the Free Press-is that what we need is a sharp economy axe instead of just a blunt penknife which I think is all that has been used up to date. If that had happened, then there could have been relief not merely for those now benefiting but for those who are ignored.
Let us look at another side of this picture. The other night I said that one of the things so unsatisfactory about this form of relief is this. It is not that the minister is going to walk off with any less of our money. He is able to throw us a little tip and still keep more of our money than he had before. He is going to take $4,473 million as compared with $4,375 million during the current year; and that is leaving out old age security payments which will be $344 million. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand this practice which the minister has-and perhaps the government has it too-of segregating in his mind old age security as if somehow it was a different kind of money, obtained by a different
2338	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell government and used for some different sort of purposes. Why on earth it should be separated I do not know. Whether they think it will lessen the pain to keep it in two parts, I do not know. To me it is merely confusing. I suggest that the practice might be abandoned. Again I say that, when the public is aware of these facts, I think it is going to take more than a little tax reduction given to someone else to keep them from complaining.
I said a moment ago that we have kept repeating that the only way to deal with this matter was to grapple with the appalling expenditures. It has often been said before but you also always hope, Mr. Speaker, that there is a last straw. There is a last straw.
I am not at all sure that this budget may not be the last straw because I think there are new circumstances. First of all, there is the Currie report which has kindled into a vigorous flame what up to the present has been merely smoldering. People are tax-angry and I do not think that anything that has happened in the last week is going to soften them up.
I do not wish to leave the impression-not for a moment-that I think it is only in the Department of National Defence that there is room for saving. I should like to recall that last year, when complaining about the overlapping of departments, I pointed out the number of economists there were, and how many departments each had their own staff of economists. I feel about that matter as I do about a great many other things, namely, that the test applied by this government has not been "What can we do without?" but, "Would it not be a nice thing to have this, that or the other thing?" I have no doubt that it is nice for every minister to have a battery of economists but I question whether it is not running us into great extravagance. I question whether, with some centralization, it could not be greatly lessened.
On looking at the estimates I find this year that there is a great array of architects. For instance, the army, navy and air force have fifteen. The Department of Agriculture apparently has five. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration has three. The Department of External Affairs has only one; I do not know what has happened to them. The Department of Justice has five; that surprises me a bit. The Department of Labour has one; the Department of Health and Welfare has one; the Department of Public Works has thirty-two; there is more reason for them there. The Department of Resources and Development has four. The Department of Transport has four and the Department of Veterans Affairs


has four. In addition to these architects, of course they have their satellites and there are several hundred draftsmen, and in addition large sums for outside professional architectural services. I think there is a lot of nonsense about this duplication. I believe it is just keeping up with the Joneses to have architects in every department.
I am glad to be able to quote the Senate finance committee on this. They appear to agree with me in this respect. While the government never seems to speak up loud and clear they did in their report of last June. They said:
The growing practice for other departments of government to by-pass Public Works Department and build up little public works branches of their own should cease.
I imagine we have one member of the government who would agree with that.

speechtext: See him smiling now.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, it is all very well for him to smile; he is good at that; but what we want to know is: What is he going to do about all these architects? The Senate had another crack to take at another practice. They were speaking of the increasing volume of publications from government departments and they said:
Your committee feels that much of this is unnecessary and useless and should be completely overhauled.
They could tell the world, Mr. Speaker, that much of this is unnecessary and useless and should be completely overhauled.
I repeat the astounding evidence that I mentioned about television the other night. I want to get this on the record again:
The C.B.C. Toronto and Montreal stations and studios cost $3 million each. But a new and powerful United States television station is now going up at Bellingham, just across the United States border from Vancouver and Victoria, at a cost of some $80,000.
That is an astounding statement. I checked it as far as I could with responsible people, and one of the responsible people gave me the interesting comment that I mentioned in the house last Thursday. He said:	"It all
depends upon the attitude you take toward money."

speechtext:
I want to say a little about other non-defence figures because we should not imagine they are small or that the increases are small. I hold in my hand a statement which shows several of the departments. The figures are for 1939-40; 1949-50 and 1953-54, in other words, four years ago and fourteen years ago. They are as follows: Civilian allowances for 193940 amounted to $1,181,090; in 1949-50 they went to $5,010,205; and in 1953-54 they are estimated at $8,780,000. Travelling and transportation: in 1939, $4,742,206; in 1949-50, $23,052,346; in 1953-54, $53,558,588. Let me head off the easy answer by saying I know that involves a good deal of transportation between Germany and Korea, but that does not begin to explain that huge rise.
Then we come to publications, films, broadcasting and advertising. In 1939 they amounted to $624,420; in 1949-50, $6,828,957; in 1953-54, $7,368,412. The next is freight, express and cartage. In 1939-40 the figure was $639,825; in 1949-50,	$8,800,686; in
1953-54, $18,790,004. For telephones, telegrams and postage we get these figures:	in
1939-40, $960,248; in 1949-50, $8,972,069 and in 1953-54, $13,002,208. There is also an additional amount of $3,899,952 for postage in 1953-54. For printing and stationery we get the figure of $2,582,901 in 1939-40, practically $14 million in 1949-50 and in 1953-54, $19,535,978. You see how these figures have shot up and the end is not yet, unless somebody comes in to take effective action.
Nobody supposes that economies are easy. These economies that we demand will not come without pressure. Where is the pressure going to come from? I submit it will not come from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The Prime Minister spoke about economy when the house assembled in November last. It seemed to me that what he was really telling us was that you could not do much about it; that it was unfortunate, but you could not do much about it. There was no sense of urgency. I understand the walls of Jericho fell down when the trumpets blew, but they must have blown hard. With deference, I feel that the Prime
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell Minister's tone was weak and quavering. He seemed to be telling us merely why it could not be done, not how it could be done.
I said that there would be nothing done except under pressure. Savings will be made when there is a real desire to make them, but this government does not will to make savings. If savings came around and jumped up in their faces, of course they would make them, but that is not the way they are made. This government does not will to make them. They are accustomed to spending, and spending is pleasant. They have had large surpluses, and in those last years they have never had a real inescapable spur to economy.
The minister takes refuge behind the total figures of interest and of national defence figures, as if these were irreducible, as if they were unchangeable, like the laws of the Medes and Persians.
Well, I am afraid we must confess that perhaps in the early months of the new defence program we may have been a little negligent in allowing that attitude to prevail, but it is gone now. That cannot go on any longer. People are beginning to reach the attitude of mind where they are utterly unwilling to accept that attitude any more.

I want to say something about tariffs. I am amazed at the things which responsible people, pursuing their conception of the party line, allow themselves to say about tariffs. We are in a controversial business. Political life is one of strife, of course, but it does seem to me that there are certain things which should not be done, even in political life. Sometimes I wonder if that is not forgotten.
I am sorry that I shall have to read this because it has a lot of detail in it. I want to say something about the tariff policy of this country, in the hope that some of the outrageously inaccurate and misleading things, even if I do not use stronger words, may perhaps no longer be said. I think it is about time somebody raised his voice to expose the campaign of misrepresentation and sham with regard to tariff policy that is carried on by a portion of the Liberal press in Canada.
Now, just where can the line in principle be drawn between the two historic parties with respect to tariff? It is a matter of history that a Conservative government made the first general increase in the Canadian tariff structure since confederation. Prior to the election of 1878 Sir John Macdonald, leading the opposition, formulated this policy on a motion to go into committee of supply. This was his amendment, and I think that, regardless of party, people will find this amendment interesting. It reads as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the welfare of Canada required the adoption of a national policy, which, by a judicious readjustment of the tariff, will benefit and foster the agricultural, the mining, the manufacturing, and other interests of the dominion; that such a policy will retain in Canada thousands of our fellow countrymen who are now obliged to expatriate themselves in search of the employment denied them at home; will restore prosperity to our struggling industries, now so sadly depressed; will prevent Canada from being made a sacrifice market; will encourage and develop an active interprovincial trade; and moving (as it ought to do) in the direction of a reciprocity of tariffs with our neighbours, so far as the varied interests of Canada may demand, will greatly tend to procure for this country, eventually, a reciprocity of trade.
I should like to repeat those last words:
-will greatly tend to procure for this country, eventually, a reciprocity of trade.
Now recall the circumstances in which this policy was set forth. The British preferences which were helpful to Canadian agriculture for generations had been repealed. The reciprocity agreement with the United States had been repealed, and the United States displayed a steadfast refusal to renew it with Liberal or Conservative governments. We come now to the 1896 election, with the Liberal party tied hand and foot by a free 68108-150i
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell trade plank which it had adopted in convention in 1893, a few years earlier. What did they do about tariffs? They adopted the Conservative national policy, hook, line and sinker, in the first budget. That is a matter of history. Next they sought to ease the conscience of newspapers like the Winnipeg Free Press by providing for a British preference which was carefully framed not to injure Canadian industry.
I come now to the reciprocity campaign of 1911. Do the members of this house realize that on that occasion the Liberal government then in power refused to offer to the United States the intermediate tariff, except on a few inconsequential items? The defeat of reciprocity was followed by the Underwood tariff, 1913, which gave Canada free entry into the markets of the United States on products of the farm as well as other raw products.
Here is another fact that some hon. members may have forgotten. We had a Conservative administration in power for ten years under Sir Robert Borden and Arthur Meighen. What did they do with this Laurier tariff which was hailed by the Liberals in 1896 as a free trade tariff? Except for some war revenue duties, which were promptly repealed after the war was over, they left it entirely unchanged. It was good enough from the point of view of giving protection to Canadian industry for Sir Robert Borden and Arthur Meighen.
Then we come to a different era. The Underwood tariff was repealed in 1922. It was succeeded by the Fordney-McCumber tariff in the same year which served to exclude Canadian farm products from the United States. In the face of this a Liberal administration sat with its hands folded for nearly ten years. Then came the Hawley-Smoot tariff in June 1930, when the Liberals were still in power, and demolished such trade in farm products as was permitted under the previous tariff measures. The United States did not stop there. On top of the Hawley-Smoot they passed the emergency tariff act in 1932 which placed special duties against our copper and lumber.
It is in these circumstances, and in this atmosphere, that R. B. Bennett made his proposal to the British and all other governments of the empire. These resulted in providing Canada at the time with a sheltered market, especially in Britain. But Mr. Bennett did not stop there. He made a definite proposal for a trade agreement with the United States, and in his proposal he included what Mr. Fielding would not include in 1911, an offer of the intermediate tariff. Up to this time, no Canadian leader or other statesman had dreamt of offering the intermediate tariff

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell to the United States. This resulted in a trade agreement made between Canada and the United States in November, 1935, thirteen days after the King government was returned to power. What they really did was to sign on the dotted line the agreement that had been on the point of being signed while Bennett was still in office.
It is true that in 1930 the Bennett government had made substantial increases in the Canadian tariff right across the board. Rightly or wrongly, he did what practically all countries in the world were doing, including Britain, for the first time in nearly three-quarters of a century, that is, taking measures to protect the national economy against the devastating fall in world prices and shrinkage in world trade.
It should be pointed out that Mr. Dunning, a Liberal minister of finance, earlier in the year 1930 had already put in tariff increases. The facts are on the record for anyone to read about this 1935 agreement, but let me give you what some may regard as appropriate confirmation of the statement I have just made. Mr. Bruce Hutchison, in his interesting biography "The Incredible Canadian", had this to say at page 216:
Three weeks after the election, he (Mr. King) redeemed his first campaign promise by closing a trade agreement with the United States to reduce Canadian and American tariffs. The agreement was far more important for its long-range intent than for its immediate results, and represented a drastic change in the high policies of both countries.
Then again, Mr. Hutchison says:
The retreat from Ottawa, (i.e. from the Ottawa agreements), continued to the eve of the 1935 election when Bennett had negotiated and was almost ready to sign a tariff-reducing agreement with Roosevelt-on taking office King found that agreement ready to his hand. He promptly signed it with a few amendments. It was Bennett's work, a work denying his original principles, but no less valuable for that.
The much maligned national policy of tariff of Sir John Macdonald became a cornerstone of Liberal policy and after that unilateral tariff reduction as far as this country was concerned was at an end.
Then we come to the next most important step. We come frankly to what has been described as bargaining tariffs. Mr. Bennett, owing to his bargaining position which he secured through the empire agreements, was able to secure market opportunities in the United States. Mr. King pursued this policy, and in 1938 made trilateral agreements, by which the concessions we had in the United Kingdom were traded off for comparable concessions in the United States. That then is the policy of this government, a policy of increasing trade by mutual or by multilateral agreements. So, just as the Laurier
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1

government had stolen the clothes of the government of Sir John Macdonald, this government proudly wears the bargaining tariff clothes of the Bennett government.
All members of this house accept this policy. We have virtually all stood by the Geneva agreement and the Torquay and Annecy agreements; and there is at the present time no great difference in principle between the parties in this house with respect to tariffs. When, however, we take stock of the actual facts, we find that the present government are using customs and excise and various forms of imposition to raise prices unconscionably. To illustrate, I am referring to figures from the Winnipeg Free Press which deal with an automobile imported from the United States at $2,000.
First we must take the customs duty of 174 per cent. This amounts to $350. The succeeding levies are then pyramided. First the importer pays a special excise tax-as is also paid on the Canadian make-of 15 per cent. Here we have another $352.50 which brings the laid-down price up to $2,702.50. Do we stop there? Not a bit of it. There is a general sales tax of 10 per cent on the marked-up price as it then stands or on the sum of $2,702.50. This comes to an additional $270.25. Where is the buyer at now? His $2,000 imported car has reached the grand total of $2,972.75, of which $972.75 goes into the pocket of the government.
I must acknowledge to the house that, to my amazement, the Free Press in its evangelistic eagerness has made a technical mistake. I have made inquiries and I find that the sales tax is not pyramided on the special excise tax, so that the calculation, instead of as the Winnipeg Free Press works it out, would work out in this way. On the $2,000 imported car you first pay 174 per cent customs duty, and that brings the mark-up to $2,350. You next pay on that mark-up the 15 per cent special- excise and the 10 per cent sales tax which is 25 per cent, so that exactions amount to $587.50. So the mark-up price is not as the Free Press figures it out to be, $972.75, but is $937.50.
Now let us see the rate on the family car in Bennett's day. Today the $2,000 car is the ordinary businessman's car. In the 1920's and 1930's the ordinary family car and the ordinary businessman's car never exceeded $1,200 in value. As a matter of fact, on the import level $1,200 would represent a fairly good car. Now what do we find? When Mr. Bennett came into power in 1930, an imported car at not more than $1,200 retail carried the following rates of duty: British preference, 124 per cent; intermediate, 174 per cent;

general, 20 per cent. So at that time the general tariff against automobiles applied to the United States was 20 per cent.
Mr. Bennett, in his tariff changes in the special session of 1930, did not touch those rates. He did, however, increase the rates on those cars selling in excess of $1,200; that is in excess of what we all know was then the value of the ordinary family car. But what were the rates in the terrible Bennett days on the $1,200 car which corresponds to the $2,000 car of today? There were 20 per cent customs tax, 5 per cent excise and never more than 6 per cent general sales tax. That is a total of 31 per cent.
What are the rates now on the ordinary family car? They are as follows: customs, 17J per cent; special excise, 15 per cent; general sales tax, 10 per cent. They are 42J per cent, or 11J per cent more than the highest rates ever levied by any Conservative government in this country.
Mr. Speaker, you will be glad to know that I am nearly through, but I want to read to this house a statement from the Winnipeg Free Press. Then having regard to what I have read, I want the members to consider this and to consider whether it is the kind of thing that a responsible journal should write. It seems to me that it is a monstrous misrepresentation of the facts which are on record and which everybody-particularly a newspaper that seeks to lead public opinion- should know. I read from the Free Press of January 16, 1953:
The present Canadian tariff, although but a shadow of the old Conservative tariff, is still much too high . . . The Conservative party stands for protection. As shown the present over-all Liberal protection on automobiles is about 22 per cent. Contrast this with Conservative policy. In the last Conservative parliament, 1930-35, the tariff on all automobiles priced at $2,100 or less was 30 per cent, and on all higher-priced cars 40 per cent. And then, as now, there was an excise tax and sales tax which pyramided the actual tariff rate. There is absolutely no hope of tariff reform from the Conservative party. It is steeped and indurated m protection. High tariffs are the only policy to which, down the years, the party has been faithful.
In the light of the facts that I have brought forward this afternoon, I ask if there is a scintilla of justification for that statement and whether it is not, in any man's language, a gross misrepresentation of fact. I bring that forward because this kind of talk that I have read is common. It is used by people sometimes, I believe, in sincere ignorance and sometimes in insincere malice. I think it is desirable that this should be on the record. I only wish I could shout it into the ears of every Canadian.
Before I take my seat I want to say just a word about dominion-provincial relations.
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell The minister dealt with this topic in traditional fashion; and when I say "traditional fashion", I mean the tradition now established by the government. He seemed to show considerable self-satisfaction with regard to what had happened. It seemed to me, however, that he left out of consideration entirely one important factor. I do not think the word "municipality" was even mentioned in his speech, but I think municipalities cannot be ignored much longer. The dominion at the present time takes 71-7 per cent-that is for the fiscal year ended March, 1952-the municipalities 10-9 per cent and the provinces 17-4 per cent of the total take. An extremely interesting speech was made in this house by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) some little time ago in which, with all the experience of municipal life which he has had, he pointed out the plight of Pickering municipality which is near Toronto. Pickering is an old community and I would have thought that it was one of the best, most stable and solid communities that one could know. Yet the hon. member for Ontario pointed out that Pickering was not able to have a water supply and that during the recent drought water had to be delivered in tanks.
It could be answered, "Why should not Pickering pay for a water supply if it wants one?" That brings me to the question which I think the minister has ignored but which I do not think can be ignored for much longer. There was a time, not so long ago, when the municipalities' share of the total tax dollar was 39-4 per cent. It is now 10-9 per cent. That tells a story, Mr. Speaker, and it is a story that I think we are going to have to listen to before long.
Just a word now about the broader question. This question, of course, takes us back to dominion-provincial conferences; it takes us back to what happened in these buildings in 1946; and takes me back particularly to what the premier of Nova Scotia said at that time. I was interested to find that just the other day he had really reiterated his views and put us on notice as to what is the real inwardness or the real implication of this problem which we have not yet solved. Speaking to the students at Dalhousie university law school in October last, he asked:
Do we wish to continue as a federal state?
And continued:
I express no choice at this time, as between a unitary state and a federal state. I do say that certain things done over the last 30 or so years show a trend toward the unitary state. Thus about 1900 the federal government went into the labour field, in 1917 the income tax field; 1918, health; 1926, old age pensions; 1941, unemployment insurance; 1944, family allowances.
2348	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
Today one sees the central government extending its influence and its money into such matters as the building of hospitals, the support of education, the construction of highways. Most of these have been traditionally, and in many cases constitutionally, matters of purely provincial concern.
Under its unrestricted power to tax . . . the central government is, of course, in a very strong financial position. That position is further strengthened by the tax rental agreements, so-called, entered into by the central government and most of the provinces.
One does not need to be an expert in the arts of divination to realize that Mr. Macdonald is troubled and perplexed about the situation, and how can anyone avoid being troubled about a matter which is handled so that the province of Quebec is an absentee from the council table? How can we be content to go on? The government is fond of reminding us of their great representation from the province of Quebec, but it seems to me that their representation is not doing them very much good at the present time. What is happening is that we have horsetrading agreements

the minister used a different word the other night-sometimes shotgun agreements, where one province is played off against another and there is in certain cases what can best be described as an uneasy truce.
Dans la province de Quebec, le probleme de la centralisation des pouvoirs fiscaux a Ottawa a produit une resistance bien deter-minee. Pour les citoyens de la province de Quebec, la question ne se pose pas sous forme de gain ou de perte en argent; il s'agit de maintenir intacts les droits provin-ciaux qu'ils ont toujours conserves jalouse-ment et qu'ils envisagent bien au-dessus de toutes considerations materielles. Sans doute, 1'exemple du Quebec nous porte tous a reflechir et a nous rendre compte que la question des relations federates provinciates se rattache, comme l'a dit M. Angus Macdonald, a celle de l'Etat unitaire, dans toute son ampleur. Par consequent, c'est une question qui touche a la racine meme de la vie et de la citoyennete canadienne, comme les a congues la Confederation.
What I have been trying to say in my indifferent French, Mr. Speaker-I have not had, like you, the advantage of being at Laval university-is that in the province of Quebec the problem of centralization of taxing power at Ottawa has produced a very definite resistance. To the citizens of Quebec the matter is not merely one of more or less money but of the maintenance intact of the provincial rights which they have always jealously preserved and which they regard as far above mere material considerations.


Indeed, the example of Quebec may well have an influence on the rest of us in making us realize that the question of dominion-provincial relations really does bring in, as Mr. Angus Macdonald said, the whole question of the unitary state and therefore goes to the very root of Canadian life and citizenship as set up by confederation.
I shall not trespass on your patience longer, Mr. Speaker. I end where I began. This is a bad budget. The minister speaks of the "social dividend", but what he should have called it is an "anti-social dividend" inasmuch as it has done virtually nothing for 75 per cent of the earners of this country- those whose need is greatest. The minister has thought of everyone except the people. We say that if it had not been for profuse waste and extravagance he could have done something for the people too. But the government refuses to take the first step to end wholesale waste and profusion, which is to extend the Currie inquiry. Could anything better illustrate the pass to which we have come? We in this house in the opposition have exhausted our efforts. It now remains for public opinion to step in. We saw a year ago in connection with a public works bill, which was radically changed after being introduced in this house, that public opinion can bring this government to its knees in no time. Let us see to it that before this budget debate is over the public is fully informed. If they are, we need have no doubt of the result. They will demand action.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross);
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that under the present budget the government proposes to take more money from the taxpayers of Canada than ever before for non-defence and defence expenditures without any effective steps being taken to:
(a)	deal with waste, extravagance and administrative inefficiency;
(b)	give tax relief to those who need it most;
(c)	offer any encouragement to Canadian farmers in meeting the serious consequences of lost markets and lower prices resulting from the government's agricultural and marketing policies;
(d)	permit an independent inquiry into the organization accounting and administration of the Department of National Defence."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be able once again to participate in the debates in this house. In doing so on this occasion I want to congratulate the minister on the budget statement. I did not hear it, but I had the opportunity of reading it, and as an outline of the position of the country it does a great deal of credit to him. I am very happy to say that.

I want to join the hon. member for Greenwood in expressing sympathy to the family of Dr. Clark. In the death of the deputy minister of finance Canada lost another great public servant. I am sure all hon. members realize the extent to which he gave of his very best to the welfare of his country.
I propose to stick pretty close to the budget this afternoon. There are some matters I should like to discuss. I should like to say something about the Currie report. I am not refraining from saying something about the Currie report because I think it would be out of order to do so. This is an omnibus debate, and one could deal with almost anything in it provided he did not refer specifically to something that had been said in a previous debate in the house.
With regard to the budget I have noticed that the press has described it as an election budget. I suppose it was intended to be an election budget, but I cannot see that there is anything in the budget for the great mass of the Canadian people. In fact, the feature of the budget is that it actually discriminates against the low-income group in our country. In making the tax concessions that have been made the minister has failed completely to apportion those concessions in such a way as to benefit the vast majority of our Canadian citizens.
He informs us that he had about $250 million in this coming fiscal year to devote to tax relief and he credits this sum, and I think quite properly, to increased production, efficiency and plain hard work on the part of a united Canadian people. Those are his own words, and I certainly agree with that statement. He then tells us that the relief he proposes is a real social dividend, well and truly earned by our people. But when it comes to apportioning the social dividend and rewarding Canadians for the virtues he has mentioned, he forgets the great bulk of the Canadian people who actually toil to make this dividend possible. Most of his tax concessions go, instead, to the well to do in this country, and particularly to those whose incomes are derived from corporation and stock dividends. And I shall have something more to say about that in a moment.
This may be a social dividend budget; but I am afraid it can be shown-and I shall try to show it-that it is for the rich, rather than for the average Canadian. We have no choice but to come to the conclusion that it is a rich man's budget, when we compare the total concessions made to the average Canadian with the total concessions made to the well to do.
The Budget-Mr. Caldwell
Let us take a look. If we concede-and may I say it is making a generous concession to the minister and the government when you do concede it-that only Canadians in the lower income brackets will benefit from the changes made in the medical expense allowance, in the reduction of the tax on cigarettes, in the abolition of the radio licence fee, and, we will say, half of the benefits resulting from a reduction in the personal income tax-if, as I say, we make that concession, then the total for this coming year in benefits to the lower income groups in Canada, with incomes of, let us say, $5,000 or less, would be $75,500,000.
Now, doing the same sort of thing-and not entirely accurately of course, but I think quite fairly-on the other hand we may say that the well to do are given the following relief: First of all, a reduction in the corporation tax; increased credit for dividends; and, as I took the other half just now, we will credit to this group also half of the reduction in the personal income tax; abolition of the tax on cheques which, of course, are used chiefly by those people in the country who are better off, and the abolition of the tax on security transfers. If we add all these together we get a grand total of $167,500,000.
In other words, those whom I have classified as the better off and wealthier people in our society will receive 70 per cent of the tax reductions, while Canadians in the lower income brackets will obtain 30 per cent only of those reductions. But even this ratio of 70:30 is giving the minister the benefit of the doubt; for most of the well-to-do people will benefit also from the tax concessions given to the small-income Canadians. On the other hand few small-income Canadians will benefit from the tax concessions made to those whom I have classified as the well to do or rich.
We in the C.C.F. party have always held to the principle that the imposition of taxes should be in accordance with ability to pay. It seems to me the minister has applied this principle in reverse. Instead of making such generous concessions to those who do not need them, he could have granted relief to Canadians of limited means in quite a number of ways.
For example, he could have raised the income tax exemption levels; he could have amended the social security tax by removing the $60 ceiling and graduating it according to ability to pay. He could have abolished the 4 per cent floor on medical expenses. He could have reduced the general sales and special excise taxes.
But he did none of these things. He preferred to grant the more substantial relief
2350	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell to corporations, corporation shareholders, and to the shareholders of Canadian companies. Then, without offering any apologies, the minister gave preferential treatment to corporations, over individuals, by making the tax reduction for corporations retroactive to January 1, 1953. But when he came to the tax reductions for individuals he did not make them effective until July 1-six months later.
And when we examine these so-called tax reductions for lower-income Canadians we begin to wonder just what reductions the minister is talking about. For example let us take, as did the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the Canadian family of average size. Let us consider the average taxpayer with two children who earns $2,400 a year and who, in 1950 paid $19, including his social security tax.

I should have said 1952. In 1953 the same taxpayer will pay $18, or a mere saving of one dollar to be spread over a twelve-month period. Or take the case of the married taxpayer with two children earning $3,000. In 1952 he paid $130, including social security tax, whereas in 1953 he will pay $126, or will make a saving of $4. This is a reduction of only 3 per cent, on an average, or 33 cents a month. That is his gain. That is the contribution this budget makes to his family budget.
On the other hand we find a different story when we examine the savings for those in the upper income brackets. The taxpayer in the same family category receiving an income of $20,000 will benefit in 1953 to the extent of a saving of $360. In other words those in the upper income brackets will benefit most, in actual dollars, from the minister's personal income tax reduction.
More striking still is the fact that while the minister refuses to raise the exemption levels on personal income tax, the benefits to those receiving dividends from Canadian companies, by increasing their credit against personal income tax from 10 per cent to 20 per cent, are very substantial, as I shall attempt to show in a moment.
Of all the tax concessions the minister has made for the well to do in this and in previous budgets, without doubt this is the most incredible. And I think very few hon. members realize just how incredible it is. It means, for example, that a married man with no dependents who receives all his income from dividends-that is, he does nothing to increase the wealth of the country


by his labour, by his ability or his ingenuity -who receives all his income merely by receiving cheques from Canadian corporations and companies, is exempted from paying personal income tax until he is receiving $9,760 before exemptions have been made. But if this $9,760, before exemptions, were earned other than from dividends the taxpayer would be liable to income tax payment of $1,952; but because he is a shareholder in Canadian companies and receives all his income from that source, he does not pay a single cent of personal income tax.
That is an almost incredible statement; but I wish to show that it is so. I have in my hand a personal individual income tax form. I have worked it out going back from the exemption. Here is a married person with no dependents. All his income is from investments in Canadian companies or corporations.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Investments in stock in Canadian corporations, not bonds.

speechtext: In stock, yes.

speechtext: Dividend paying stock; that is an important qualification.

Quite right. From his investments in such dividend paying stocks he receives $9,760 so that his net income is $9,760. He has of course the usual deduction on personal exemption of $2,000. Deducting the $2,000 that would mean taxable income of $7,760 if it were earned. He would pay income tax on an earned income in this way. On the first $6,000 he would pay $1,140. On the remaining $1,760, where the tax is on the basis of 26 per cent, he would pay $457.60, making a total of $1,597.60. Then he would have to pay the social security tax of $60 or a total of $1,657.60 if it were earned.
This man of course would have a surtax on investment income over $2,400. He has an exemption of $2,400, and if we deduct that from $9,760 he has to pay the surtax on $7,360 at the rate of 4 per cent, which would mean that he would pay $294.40. Therefore the total tax would be $1,952 if he were paying it on the basis of earned income. But since he gets this money unearned, from other sources, from stock dividends, he is entitled to deduct 20 per cent of $9,760 or $1,952 from the tax he would otherwise have to pay. That is the exact amount that he would have paid as personal income tax if he had earned it. In other words, this gentleman who does nothing by his labour to assist the welfare of the country, who toils not and neither does he spin, pays no personal income tax.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What a budget!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is paid at the rate of 50 per cent as the result of his interest in the companies.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just a minute. Is the hon. gentleman going to argue that he has paid something? He has paid nothing, and so far as the companies in which he is interested are concerned they pass on any tax assessed against them to the general public. The general public pays that tax which this gentleman escapes in his personal income tax. I think that is a fairly complete answer to the minister's suggestion. We have asked from time to time that the personal income tax exemption level should be raised from $1,000 to $1,500 for a single person and from $2,000 to $3,000 for married persons. We have been refused this concession again and again and have been told that it would involve a loss of revenue.
But what has the government done in effect? It has doubled what I might call the exemptions, though that word perhaps does not exactly fit the situation, for an already privileged group, those who do not have to work but receive all their income from dividends in certain types of Canadian investments. This particular group is given special exemption levels and, as I have already shown by actual reference to the income tax form, they are allowed to receive up to $9,760 from investments in Canadian stocks before they pay any personal income tax. I say that indicates very clearly that this budget, apart from everything else, is not a poor man's budget. It is a rich man's budget. When I began to work this out I must confess to the minister that it seemed almost incredible to me, but I am quite sure that the example I have given is correct because I have had it checked not by one or two people but by several economists and accountants.

Nor did the minister hesitate to benefit the corporations by increasing their income bracket to which the lowest tax rate applies. Instead of the lowest tax rate applying only to the first $10,000 taxable income with the top rate applying to the remainder, the minister has increased the corporation income tax bracket to which the lowest rate applies to $20,000. As an additional concession to the corporations, he has reduced the lowest rate from 20 per cent to 18 per cent and the top rate from 50 per cent to 47 per cent. These concessions are indeed most generous and contrast strangely with what the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and I have shown to be the very niggardly concessions the minister has made to the great majority of the Canadian people.
How valuable these concessions are can be illustrated, I think, by reference to a few corporations, to see how they will benefit.
I might say that the figures are the latest we could obtain and are taken from the Financial Post survey of industrials. If we look at International Nickel, for example, on the basis of the old 1952 rates they would have paid $55,509,145 in 1951. Under the new basis they would pay $52,185,016, or a saving of $3,324,129. On Thursday the minister told us exactly the same sort of thing. In the same speech he informed us that investment in capital goods, equipment and resource development was higher last year than in 1951. Of course the figures show that to be the case, according to his budget. He has estimated that the gross national product for 1952 increased in terms of volume about 6 per cent over 1951 which, incidentally, is well above the annual increase over the past few years. He pointed out that for the three-year period, 1950 to 1952 inclusive, the gain in real product has been more than double that of the preceding three-year period. These are impressive gains that we are all happy about, as I am sure the minister will be the first to admit.
Consequently it is all the more difficult to understand what the minister means when he says that present taxation rates on corporations are impairing their incentive to invest and expand. Indeed, expansion over the past few years has been phenomenal in this country, particularly since the outbreak of the Korean war.
What we are saying is that the minister could have eased the tax burden on the small-income Canadian in many ways. For example, he could have done so if he had abolished the 4 per cent floor on medical expenses, making all medical costs deductible from income for taxation purposes. Indeed, he 

does make a gesture-but it is only a gesture -in this direction by reducing the 4 per cent to 3 per cent. I say that provides only negligible assistance to many Canadians who have little or no real insurance against the high costs of hospitalization and health services generally.
May I just say, lest I be misunderstood, that I am not blaming hospitals and I am not blaming the medical profession. I am not blaming nurses and others who render those health services. They are highly trained, highly efficient people working with very expensive equipment, and the rates are of necessity high. However, since the health of the population is something in which the whole community is interested, in the interests of all the community we think the costs should be spread over the entire community or, in any event, that the individual might be relieved of the costs by eliminating and not reducing to 3 per cent the 4 per cent floor for medical expenses.
We were told that the abolition of the floor would have cost about $40 million, which is less than half what the minister is going to lose as a result of reductions in corporation tax in a full year; yet the benefits that would have been received by Canadians generally would have been of real significance to most people.
Then there has been no reduction in the general sales and special excise taxes which my hon. friend from Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) mentioned. They do bear oppressively on the lower income groups, particularly. These indirect and hidden taxes seriously reduce the standard of living, often of those who can least afford to have that standard reduced farther-old age pensioners and people with large families and small incomes. Many articles -used in the home are subject to both a sales and a special excise tax, in which case the two taxes apply separately to the same value.
As I have said, these taxes apply to a wide range of household and other articles sold in this country. Because it is applied at the manufacturer's level it is a pyramiding tax. The 10 per cent rate then is misleading. When the wholesaler computes his mark-up on goods he does so on the basis of the manufacturer's price taken together with the sales tax. The retailer in turn computes his markup on the wholesale price which includes the sales tax. When the consumer buys an article he pays not only a mark-up on the cost of the goods but possibly two or three mark-ups on the sales tax as well.
We believe that the minister could have assisted the consumer, raising the consumer's

purchasing power measurably, if he had reduced substantially the general sales and other excise taxes. This would have done more to alleviate the tax burden on a majority of Canadians than anything the minister has done in his budget.
I want to express regret that the minister has not seen fit to reduce some of these petty taxes such as those on chocolate bars and soft drinks. He has done something for the smokers in reducing the tax on cigarettes, although he has not done anything for the poor man who rolls his own.

It would have involved only a relatively small loss of revenue and would have made so many people, particularly children, a good deal happier at a time when inflation and taxes impair the purchasing power of parents, demanding extra prudence in planning the family budget. The small luxuries have by necessity to be overlooked in many Canadian families.
It is with considerable regret that we find the minister still refuses to make the social security tax for old age pensions a graduated tax. We have from the start condemned the imposition of a flat rate of 2 per cent, with a maximum for all groups of $60 per year. We say this violates the principle that taxation should be imposed according to ability to pay. The inequitable nature of the present tax is fairly illustrated by the fact that a person who has a taxable income of $3,000 pays the same social security tax as a person with a taxable income of $10,000, $20,000, $100,000 or more.
Now, it is all too clear that the minister's budget gives little comfort and cheer to the small-income Canadian. His income tax reductions are so negligible that they can hardly be considered as reductions at all, yet outside of these the average Canadian receives no concessions worth mentioning. The minister had little left for the great majority of Canadians after his major concessions to corporations and the shareholders of stock companies and so on.
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
We believe, too, that most Canadians would have gladly forgone these few minor concessions that have been given-I mean the whole bulk of them-for something else, for a national health insurance program. The tax reductions given to corporations and shareholders, and indeed other reductions as well, could have been used to promote this program, thereby assisting, in a major effort, Canadians from one end of the country to the other. The amount of $250 million-and perhaps also the amount that has been built up in the Department of National Defence which could be used, over and above what we estimate-would have gone a long way toward giving the Canadian people a proper national health plan.
Nothing could be more ironical than that the budget should benefit to such a large degree those who are already well off, when there has been no provision to protect our people against the high cost of sickness. When I speak of the high cost of sickness, I am not only thinking of the high cost of sickness to the individual but I am thinking of the high cost of sickness to our country through unnecessary absence from work, cutting down the production of industry and so on. The economic loss to the country is very great. Surely the minister speaks with his tongue in his cheek when he calls this a social dividend budget, unless of course he is thinking only of the corporations and the shareholders.
I am not going to intrude upon the time allotted for private bills, Mr. Speaker, but I do want to say this. Were it not for the fact that another international conference on tariffs and trade is to be convened shortly, I would have devoted some attention to our vulnerable trade position. I am very glad indeed that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) raised the question of tariffs this afternoon. I was glad to hear him say what he did about it. In the old days I often used to say, whether correctly or incorrectly I leave the house and the country to judge, that the only difference between the Conservative and Liberal parties in those days was that the Conservatives believed in high tariffs and when they were in power the Liberals always maintained tariffs that were high. That was about the only difference between the two political parties that I used to be able to see. Don't ask me what the differences are that I see between them today, because that might be rather embarrassing.
Were it not for the fact that a new conference is being convened, I should have liked to say a great deal about the tariff situation. In my opinion, if prosperity is to be assured
2354	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell to this country, and indeed to the world, then the United States and Canada will have to sharply revise their tariff policies. As a matter of fact what we are doing in this country today is preventing our overseas customers from buying within our borders the goods they need, because they cannot sell here to get the dollars. We are preventing their recovery. North America has been giving aid to the European countries, the United Kingdom and other countries. They do not want that aid. What they want is trade in order that they may earn the dollars they require to buy the raw materials and food they need. Consequently, my own view is that the day is coming when consideration should be given to drastic reductions in tariffs or their elimination, so far as possible.
I am sure that sooner or later, Mr. Speaker, the high tariffs now in effect are going to boomerang against North America, and perhaps particularly against our own country.
I hope, therefore, that Canada will do everything possible in order to bring about a lowering of tariffs, preferably of course by international agreement. If it is not done through that means, then we shall have to do something in regard to this matter ourselves.
In summing up I want to say that I agree with those who have said it in the newspapers and elsewhere, that this is a rich man's budget. The minister had $250 million to dispose of and he disposed of it, but mostly to the wrong people. He might have used it to make a new start in health insurance. He even refused to abolish the 4 per cent floor for medical expenses. He might have raised personal income exemptions for the lower income groups, but he preferred to raise the exemptions of those who enjoy unearned dividends and of corporations. He might have reduced or abolished hidden taxes like the sales tax, which impose a burden on those least able to bear it. He refused to do so. In short, Mr. Speaker, from the point of view of the average Canadian this is a thoroughly bad budget.
I see nothing objectionable in the amendment proposed by my hon. friends to the right, but we think we want to be a little more specific in some particulars. I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"This house further regrets that the present budget is a rich man's budget which:
(1)	makes tax cuts retroactive to January 1st for corporations but not for individual Canadians;
(2)	doubles the exemption levels for the full corporation tax rate while leaving exemption levels for individual Canadians unchanged; and


(3) doubles the credits allowed to shareholders for dividends, but gives no comparable credits to those who do the work that produces the dividends.	'

Mr. Speaker, this bill reflects the desire of Swiss Reinsurance Company to share in the economic expansion of Canada. The authorized capital of the company consists of 60,000 shares of 1,000 Swiss francs par value, all of which are issued and outstanding and fully paid up. The board of the company consists, at present, of nine members, all of whom are prominent Swiss business or professional men. Mr. E. Hurlimann, formerly general

manager of the company and an outstanding authority on international reinsurance, is chairman of the board. The management of the company is entrusted to two general managers, Messrs. E. Froelich and P. Gug-genbuhl who, at this time, are visiting the company's branch office and subsidiaries in the United States of America.
The Swiss Reinsurance Company is the largest professional reinsurer in the world. More than 90 per cent of its business is derived from sources outside Switzerland. The Swiss Reinsurance Company has had, for many years, a number of reinsurance connections with Canadian companies and British and foreign companies operating in Canada. In view of the recent economic development of Canada it had been contemplated for some time to enter Canada as a licensed reinsurer by establishing a branch office, or through the medium of a domestic reinsurance company. It is now felt that, as a long-term plan, the latter solution should be adopted, and it is their desire to become a more active part of the Canadian insurance industry by creating a domestic company under the name of Canadian Reinsurance Company with head office in Toronto. The issued and paid-up capital of the company will be $1 million, Canadian, and a surplus of a further $1 million, Canadian, will be contributed. In spite of the fact that there are already a number of reinsurance companies located in Canada, they are of the opinion that a reinsurance company with the financial backing, and supported by the technical experience, of the Swiss Reinsurance Company is likely to become an important factor in the Canadian insurance market and thus of the Canadian economy.
