maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 150, to incorporate the Callow Veterans' and Invalids' Welfare League.

maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad today that some hon. members have shown enough interest in this bill to ask for an explanation, for it is my special privilege to introduce this bill to incorporate the Callow Veterans' and Invalids' Welfare League; and I may say, sir, that such a privilege as this comes only once in a lifetime. This bill has already been passed by the other place.
The object of the league is, as stated, to promote the welfare of veterans and invalids, and the purpose of this bill is to permit the league to obtain a dominion charter and broaden the sphere of its good work. Heretofore the Callow coaches confined their activities largely to Nova Scotia, but when this act is passed I can see this wonderful idea of Walter Callow spreading throughout Canada and into the United States.
The Callow coaches are designed and built to enable shut-ins, wheel-chair patients and others unable to get about, to be taken on outings of one kind or another. The coaches are equipped, among other things, with a special ramp which permits the patients to be wheeled into the coach without discom * fort. The service is not confined to institu tions, although it was conceived first for th t benefit of veterans at Camp Hill hospital in Halifax. People living at home, who ar<4

physically incapable of getting out by ordinary means, are also helped in this way.
When one considers the number of wounded veterans in our hospitals, the many sufferers from arthritis and rheumatism of one kind or another, polio victims, palsied children and others afflicted with crippling diseases, it is not surprising that in Halifax, where the project was begun, it has been hard to keep pace with the demand for the coaches. Now that the idea has been taken up in other parts of Canada it has become necessary to seek this charter.
The project is unique in itself, but most remarkable of all is the man behind it, Walter Callow. He was not only the inventor of the coach but also the organizer for its development, the promoter for its acceptance and the guiding spirit after the project was taken up by others in order to raise money and extend the service as far as possible. All this is enough and more for a person with all his faculties; but Walter, as many of you know, is blind, immobile, without legs or the use of his arms, but of indefatigable mental energy. Walter is a veteran who was critically injured in a plane crash while training for the flying corps in world war I. Attacked by the dreaded arthritis, he became completely paralysed and blind. He is unable to move but he can talk, and talk brilliantly.
Walter Callow is a legend, an example of sacrifice, thoughtfulness for others, and courage. His name is, may I go so far as to say, hallowed by those who have benefited by his Callow organization, for he personifies not only their own suffering but also triumph over suffering. Walter is immobilized completely, helpless physically, blind; added to this he has recently had both legs amputated. Small wonder that he has many times been referred to as the human log.
When Walter Callow underwent the operation for the amputation of both his legs he did so hoping that as a result he might live and be stronger to carry on this work for others. He had prepared for every eventuality and had arranged that, should he not come through, the organization would carry on. The amazing thing is that, as he came out of the anaesthetic, instead of thinking of his own welfare his first thoughts and his first question to the doctor and nurses was "Have you heard how the campaign is coming along?"
Such altruism cannot be equalled. Callow has a board of directors to whom I should like to pay tribute but I wish, at this time, to mention specially the former and present ministers of veterans affairs, the staff of Camp Hill hospital and, in particular, the nursing
Callow Welfare League sisters and the orderlies who have been most patient and attentive at all times.
Walter Callow knows that his inspiration is not within himself, but comes from a higher power. He gives many persons credit, and in this he could teach us a lesson in humility. Although blind to the world, he is not living in darkness. Walter's pleasure comes from the tales and stories he hears of the happiness he is bringing to others. He relives the few years when he had his health; a simple pleasure of the past now takes on fond memories, for Walter worked hard in his youth and this youth he has lived over many times.
On the broad of his back his indomitable spirit cannot be shaken, as evidenced when he proposed a certain program to his directors and insisted on it being put into effect. When the directors heard this they did not altogether agree with his proposal. They went to him and said: "If you put this through we will all resign." After a pause of a moment he said-and this shows the man- he said "Well, I guess I am without a board of directors."
Walter has done more for mental patients than any other group in Canada outside of the medical profession. Mental patients ordinarily are confined to hospitals or institutions, but through Walter Callow's efforts a program has been put into effect so that four hours of freedom on many days is given to these patients to sit and mix with normal people at the ball games and other sporting events. It is said that these outside contacts have helped greatly in the rehabilitation of many. Special arrangements have been made with the ball park executives, for everyone co-operates with Walter Callow. Thirty seats are reserved. These are the only mental patients in Canada so treated; at least that is my understanding.
Walter's great ambition is to provide the continent's disabled and afflicted with some of the everyday pleasures and comforts of a healthy citizen. His hope for this has never dimmed. His good works moved someone to suggest that he receive the George Medal. So you can judge the magnitude of his work. While Walter Callow, or what is left of him, is helpless, he has what it takes to accomplish things. He has faith in God, his fellow man, himself, and the magnificent work being done by his organization.
There will be no profits or cash dividends from this corporation-and perhaps it is fitting to make reference to dividends at a time when the budget debate is in progress- but there will be that inner satisfaction which

Callow Welfare League comes only when you know you have done unto others as you would have them do unto you.
If there are any questions hon. members would like to ask, I shall be pleased to answer them.

maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am happy indeed to associate myself with this bill, and to support what its sponsor has said today. I have known Mr. Callow for many years. He came from my constituency, having lived in Parrsboro and later at Advocate, 29 miles away in the extreme point of Cumberland. I knew him before he enlisted in the first great war in the air service, and knew him after he received his injury. I used to discuss his condition with the late Dr. Fillmore, who served the community for many miles around.
At one time I was in a position to call on Walter Callow more often than I can now.
I recall his having come to Halifax on one occasion for medical treatment. I must give praise to Camp Hill hospital in Halifax for what it has done for him, as well as many hundreds of others. On the occasion to which I refer he was at the hospital for treatment, before he was totally incapacitated as he is today. I was able to help arrange for a hydroplane to take him from Halifax to his home in something less than 60 minutes, and place him down within a hundred yards of his home at Advocate.
As has been said by the junior member for Halifax, this bill is proposed by Walter Callow himself. He is its inspiration; and the object of it is to promote the welfare and happiness of invalids. We note that the last section of the bill states that-
The league shall be operated without profit or gain to any of its members and all moneys received by it shall be devoted to further its objects and purposes.
Walter Callow has been interested in aiding veterans ever since he became incapacitated. He was the means of sending millions of cigarettes to the men in the services. As


has been explained by the hon. member sponsoring the bill, he is now primarily interested in these Callow coaches.
Canada has had many heroes in the armed services. There were many in the first great war, many in the second, and a lesser number in the present engagement. But I do not believe there has ever been a greater hero, so far as service given is concerned, than was Walter Callow from the time he enlisted until the present time. He is now completely incapacitated, as the junior member for Halifax has explained. Only recently he had to have both his legs amputated. He is completely blind and immobile. His application for this charter was signed only with the greatest of difficulty, because before that time he had not written a single word or line for over 23 years.
I remember that last autumn Mr. Callow had had these coaches in service for some time, and on that occasion he made them available for those who were incapacitated but who wished to attend the maritime winter fair, an event at which thousands of people gather each year. I had occasion to ride with a number in the coach who were incapacitated and in wheel-chairs. In attendance was a stewardess in uniform, and I can say that those who were being conveyed were as happy as any others attending the fair. They had not expected ever to be able to go again but, by virtue of Mr. Callow's efforts, and the efforts of those associated with him, hundreds upon hundreds of people in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have been able to attend ball games, exhibitions and other events.
I am happy to join with the sponsor of the bill in the House of Commons, as well as its sponsor in the other place; and I am sure every member in the house will join in making possible the passing of this charter. This is a most deserving application, and we would hope that its benefits would not be confined to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, but that it might spread throughout Canada and perhaps into the United States as well.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who knows Walter Callow, I should like to say a word at this time to express my admiration of the good work he is doing. I notice that he is described in the bill simply as an inventor. But, Mr. Speaker, Walter Callow is much more than that. If one had the command of language that would be appropriate at a time such as this he would go far beyond the use of such words as humanitarian and philanthropist,

and would use other words which might more properly describe the qualities possessed by this man.
May I express the regrets of my colleague the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) upon being absent from the house because of other business engagements. We know, however, that both as a private citizen and as the former minister of veterans affairs, the Minister of Labour has been interested in the work of Walter Callow and wished to pay a tribute to him.
It is most fitting that the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom) should have had the privilege of sponsoring the bill in the house. Because of his field of activities, through the board of trade and otherwise in Halifax, he has been in close association with Mr. Callow. This would be true not only of the junior member for Halifax but also of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black), both of whom have spoken so graciously and have conveyed to the house some indication of the hardships this man has overcome and the difficulties he has surmounted to do so much for humanity, first in Nova Scotia and now, in a broader sense, in Canada. And as the hon. member for Cumberland has suggested, perhaps his work will extend even to a broader field.
It is remarkable how sometimes the finer human qualities prevail over physical disabilities. In my home town of Lunenburg we have another example, in Earl Bailly, of a man who, without the use of his arms, legs or very much of the rest of his body, paints with a brush in his mouth and turns out marvellous masterpieces. He too is one of those who have risen above difficulties which I am sure would defeat many of us. He has always been able to regard the brighter side of life and to look at things in a way that contributes something to the happiness of other people.
I simply say, Mr. Speaker, that these are living demonstrations that there are satisfactions in this life over and above material rewards, and I know that all hon. members will join in passing this bill to perpetuate the work of Walter Callow through the Callow Veterans' and Invalids' Welfare League.

maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise also to express my support of the bill and to pay a tribute to Walter Callow. Although I have never met him personally, I feel that I know him very well because on many occasions I have had correspondence with him with respect to veterans' matters and I have also spoken to him on the telephone a number of times. I saw the coach that he invented in the province of New Brunswick last year and I realized, as did many others, the great benefit that it is to
Callow Welfare League returned men and crippled veterans. I want to pay tribute, as has been done so eloquently by the two hon. members who have just spoken, to his great courage, his will power and his outstanding achievements for the benefit of the veterans of the province of Nova Scotia, which benefits he now intends to extend to veterans throughout Canada.
We have often heard it said that those who suffer most best understand the needs and suffering of others. In no person has this been better exemplified than in Walter Callow. In thinking of him I think of that great woman of the United States, Helen Keller, who is known as one of the twelve greatest women of her country. In spite of the handicap of blindness and deafness she helped many thousands of blind people in her own country and many thousands throughout the world. I wish to pay this tribute to Walter Callow. I think that he stands second only to Helen Keller, and the veterans of Canada certainly owe a great debt to this very great man.

maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to speak in support of the bill introduced by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom). I am not conversant with the projects sponsored by Mr. Callow but the sponsor has explained how worthy they are, and I am sure the passage of the bill will have a great deal to do with the alleviation of the pain and suffering of persons who have been invalided.
In Ontario a great deal of work along this line is being done by Rotary clubs, the Canadian Legion and other service organizations. They convey invalids to places of entertainment, athletic events and other amusement centres. I am sure that a conveyance of this kind will mean much to them in the transportation of persons who are unable to take care of themselves.
I might ask a question of the junior member for Halifax. I should like to know whether Mr. Callow has any objective with respect to the number of coaches he hopes to provide. I should not like to see them limited only to one part of the country but rather made available to every province in Canada.

Callow Welfare League
In the first place, because of the suffering he has undergone, the sacrifice he has made and the burden of physical disability he has endured, a burden which would have crushed an ordinary man, this individual has shown all Canadians that a spirit -of fortitude and courage can triumph over almost any physical disability. For that reason we have respected and honoured him for many years.
In the second place we pay tribute to him because of the mechanical devices to which he has given support, the coach and the chairs which he has developed. I have seen the coach in operation in the valley during the apple blossom festival and on other occasions. The coach has come down to the valley with crippled veterans who otherwise could not have been moved from a bed. One realizes too the widened scope and wider horizons which, by his own courage and imagination, he has created for others who perhaps are hardly less fortunate than himself.
Through the introduction of this bill he is attempting now, and properly so, to give a degree of permanence to his achievements and wider scope to his operations. I am sure I speak for all Canada, as have those who have spoken before, in paying tribute to a man who could not be crushed, whose spirit is indomitable and who, by his example and by the leadership he has shown, is making a real contribution to veterans and others who have suffered and whom this house should support.

maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to join briefly in the debate. First of all I wish to congratulate my colleague from Halifax on the manner in which he presented this important piece of private legislation to the house. He covered the work of Walter Callow very well indeed. Other speakers, including the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), have filled in some of the details with which he was not able to deal.
The story of Walter Callow is one of the most amazing bits of personal history of which this country can boast. His condition of almost complete paralysis plus blindness renders him by all ordinary standards an almost hopeless invalid. Yet the record of achievement of Walter Callow over the past fifteen or twenty years is one of which the most active person in this country, a person most fully endowed with all his senses and faculties, might well be proud.
Besides Walter Callow's activities in connection with the wheel-chair coach, he was very active during the war in arranging for comforts and advantages for our troops overseas. He thought up devices and ran the


Walter Callow cigarette bank which provided hundreds of thousands of smokes for the troops overseas. He has the kind of imagination that enabled him to invent a combined knife, fork and spoon for the use of incapacitated people which has been adopted as the best available instrument of that kind in a number of institutions which care for people who have lost one or both of their arms or are otherwise incapacitated.
He thought up not only the whole idea of a wheel-chair coach, but he thought out and described to people who could put them down on paper the specifications and all the details of the construction of this coach. He thought out a very ingenious method for a hydraulic ramp at the back which would also be the main door of the coach. When it was submitted to mechanics and engineers it was said by them to be impractical and that it would not work. Walter Callow insisted that it would work and was able, by the force of his personality, to get a prototype built; and to the surprise of everybody but Walter Callow the ramp worked, and worked magnificently. It has been the basic feature that makes these coaches unique, so unique that the dominion patent office, after a proper application, granted a patent to Walter Callow for this device which he had created, not from experiment, not from experience but simply from the power of intellect and thought.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is not always possible in this world and this life for credit to be given where credit is due, but this is one occasion in this house when all speakers who have joined in this debate have had the happy privilege, in which I am so glad to join, of giving the greatest and warmest possible tribute to a human being, Walter Callow, for what he has achieved. This house will be doing itself honour and will be doing a service to the people of this country, particularly those in other parts of Canada who will benefit from the extension of operations of the Callow Veterans' and Invalids' Welfare League into other parts of Canada, by approving this legislation.

maintopic: CALLOW VETERANS' AND INVALIDS' WELFARE LEAGUE
speechtext:
Briefly I just want to associate myself with the previous speakers. I have known Walter Callow personally for 30 years. I think he is a living demonstration of the power of mind over matter. I also think the fact that he is still alive and able to do what he is doing reflects with considerable credit on the Camp Hill hospital. He must have received and did receive excellent care during the long period he has been in that institution.
I think it was George Bernard Shaw who said that the hereafter is composed of the

things you leave behind you, the monuments that you have erected demonstrating the fact that you have lived and contributed something to society during the time that you did live. I am very happy to be here and to lend my voice to the praises of Walter Callow that have already been put on the record by previous speakers. There is no need to repeat them. I think the coach he has developed under the difficulties he has had to contend with will live as a monument to the memory of Walter Callow long after he has departed this world.

Mr. Speaker, most of the members in the house today are not privileged to come from the maritimes. However, I am sure we all approve of the justifiable pride which the members from the maritimes, who have spoken in this debate, have shown in the accomplishments of this distinguished Nova Scotian.
I rise to add a few words, in the first place because I believe that Walter Callow really belongs to the whole of Canada, and in the second place because I have never known anyone with greater selflessness, greater determination or greater courage.
A good many years ago he started to write to me about the problems of veterans. Then five or six years ago I had the privilege of visiting him in Camp Hill hospital in Halifax and learning of his plans for this wheel-chair coach for veterans and invalids. Throughout all this time his whole attitude has been one of serving other people and not worrying about his own disabilities which are perhaps as great as those of anyone in Canada today.
Now he is asking for the incorporation of a dominion company so he can spread his good works right across this nation. For example, he has telephoned me twice this month concerning plans for a coach in British Columbia. I have no doubt that he has similar plans for each one of the provinces. I am very glad to be able to support the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom) today and to congratulate him for sponsoring this bill.
Finally, I believe that Walter Callow is setting a standard of service which cannot be excelled, and that he is one of the great Canadians of our time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks tonight I should like to associate myself with what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said in his budget address on last Thursday evening in connection with Dr. Clark, the late deputy minister of finance. I should like to join with the minister in expressing keen and deep regret at the sudden passing of a great public servant.

Last Thursday night, Mr. Speaker, there was great jubilation amongst the Liberals. Judging from the way they applauded they probably thought that the jaunty, good-natured Minister of Finance had dragged the party corpse out of the fishing pond at Peta-wawa and had breathed the breath of life back into it. The minister himself thought so, I think, before he romped to the climax of his peroration and made his final flourish before he sat down. I venture to say that when the self-induced hypnosis had passed- for that is just what it was-say, by Sunday, the corpse was still a corpse. The buoyancy that was generated by frantic Liberal party hopes that the peace offerings in the budget would be gratefully received by the Canadian electors and that all the past would be forgotten, was only momentary and fleeting. Since Saturday there have been unmistakable signs throughout the country and in the press that when the taxpayers sat down with their pencils sharpened and some paper in front of them, in the calm hours after the uproar that took place in the house, three pointed conclusions stabbed their consciousness and left them cold. These are the three, in my judgment.
The first is that the minister's budget was overrated as far as individual material benefit is concerned. In this respect I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) who stated this afternoon that this was the rich man's budget and that there was little in it for the little man, the ordinary fellow. That is the conclusion most of the people throughout the country have reached. But let me say this. The minister never before in his whole life did such a fine job of making a thing look good. I pay him that tribute; he made it look good.
The second conclusion that people have reached, with pencil in hand, is that this is a great appeasement budget. As skilful as the minister is, he was not able to conceal the fact that he was making a supreme effort to buy less hostility toward a guilty government. He touched, however lightly in some cases, nearly every pocketbook in the Dominion of Canada. A government that is a real friend of the people, that through the years between elections has dispensed justice and equity, and that has shown a high measure of integrity and concern over the welfare of the people, need never resort to such transparent measures of appeasement just before an election. The taxpayers are wise enough to know that their friends are those who stand by them through all the years with the best that there is to offer. For example-and I commend this example to hon. members-the Social Credit government of
The Budget-Mr. Low
Alberta has not once in nearly eighteen years resorted to an appeasement budget in order to try to gloss over blunders or maladministration.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will just take that phrase as well, "or if production increased". I should like to have the minister, in his rebuttal, tell us how much increase in production there has been since then. This was last October.
Millions of Canadians are wise to this old political game with the people's taxes. The Liberals held out hope of reductions in taxes after a Liberal defeat last year. They discouraged the hope after Liberal successes, and now they make a few small reductions just before a general election to catch the unwary. They did it in 1949 in a shameless manner. The electors of Canada will be perfectly justified in condemning this government for playing a game definitely designed to fool the public. I make this statement with full knowledge of my responsibility as a member in this house. The tax burden could have been materially reduced in each of the past two years without in any way interfering with essential services or with the defence program. The entire sales tax could have been abolished two or three years ago, with a consequent substantial reduction in the cost of living.
I want to emphasize with all I have at my command that there has been absolutely no reason, no necessity for the continuing high taxes over the years. There could have been relief for the people two or three years ago, as the substantial year-end surpluses testify. Let me remind the members of the house that these surpluses were accumulated even in the face of a breakdown of control in the army works services; even in the face of refusal by government departments to curtail their competitive spending at a time when rigid economy was needed for the purpose of giving the defence effort top priority in materials, manpower and funds; and even in the face of waste and extravagance that has run throughout the whole defence department 
and several departments of government. It has seemed to me as though every conscious effort was being made in various departments to cause surpluses to disappear for the express purpose of maintaining the government in a position to launch this great appeasement just before the general election.
May I give as just one example of what looked to me like a patent attempt at getting rid of an embarrassing surplus of cash, the way this repointing job was done on this very building last fall. Some of you may have seen it. I watched it day after day as the work proceeded. Much of that work was done at a time and under conditions when it would be sheer waste. The mortar cement was still being put in between the stones when heavy frosts were occurring at night, and sometimes during the day, frosts that would crumble the green material and cause it to drop out long before its time. The total amount of that contract and the real value the people got for the money spent would be a most revealing bit of study for the members of this house.
Well, the Liberal government has tried all the tricks over the years. I do not know that there are any new ones, but short as the memories of the people are, after so many repetitions they are getting fed up and wised up, because they fully expect that if the Liberals were to be returned to power it would not be long before taxes were up again just as happened after 1949. The theme song of the Canadian taxpayer today is "If you loved me half as much as I love you", and I emphasize the last line: "You build me up only to let me down." People do learn though, by experience, especially repeated experience.
Just a word about the income tax reductions; I feel about them much as was expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I had my pencil going for several days working out some schedules that were almost identical with those he presented here this afternoon. I do not intend to weary the house by a repetition, but do let me say this. What he gave this afternoon as an analysis of the income tax changes was exactly right. I doubt whether he would be more than one or two dollars out in his calculations, and the picture he showed is something for the Canadian people to think about. But the Liberal press across the country played it up as a real slash. Boy, what a cut! Actually individuals will pay a little less this year than they paid last year.
The minister took great care to make the reductions for individuals effective on July 1.

Of course, Mr. Speaker, this means not only that the individual taxpayer will enjoy only the 5J per cent reduction this year, but it will also mean that if the Liberals manoeuvre things just about right the first cheques with the lower income tax deductions will be in the hands of the taxpayers about the time they go to the polls.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government will argue, of course, that next year is the time the people will really get the benefit of the full 11 per cent reduction provided in the budget. In reply I should like to point out that this budget governs only this year. Next year will be governed by another budget entirely and the situation may be entirely different by then. Judging by past experience I should say the Canadian taxpayers had better do their calculating on what they have got this year and enjoy it while they can, because the whole business can be changed with a stroke of the minister's pen when he drafts another budget. The Liberal party has never impressed anyone yet as having stood for rock-bottom taxes; just the contrary is the case, as a matter of fact.
Now a word about corporation taxes. It is quite amazing how keen and penetrating the minister's perception can become in an election year. You know one can go along for years entirely oblivious to the ill effects of tax policies and then quite suddenly become as fully aware of the evils as though you had known them all the time. I would not suggest of course that imminence of a test at the polls would have anything to do with that keener perception on the part of my genial friend the Minister of Finance; not at all. But seriously, the minister showed commendable concern about what his high tax has been doing to Canadian corporations. We have been trying to tell him all along that his taxation policies were ruining business and he as much as admitted it in his splendid speech the other night. As a consequence he allocated half his tax largesse to them. They are to get $120 million of relief this year out of a total tax reduction of $250 million. That is a pretty fair slice.
Well, the minister's concern for the corporations is commendable, even if it does come a little late. We do need healthy corporations in Canada, and if we are going to continue on a private enterprise kind of economy these corporations must be able to make a reasonable profit, one that will enable them to stay in business and accumulate savings or undistributed profits sufficient to provide for the necessary expansion of plant and replacement of machinery to keep the economy robust and thriving. But I would
The Budget-Mr. Low
like to ask the minister how much profit they need to make. After paying their costs, and their taxes, and a fair and encouraging dividend to the shareholders, how much undistributed profits do they need?
That is quite a question. My calculations show me that Canadian corporations, in the ten-year period between 1940 and 1950 inclusive, accumulated undistributed profits of $4,952 million in round figures. That was after paying all their costs and in addition dividends of $4,276 million, and also after setting aside total depreciation allowances of $6,338 million. I have not the figures for 1951 and 1952, but I would judge from what I have read and observed that accumulations for those two years would be more than the average of the previous ten, so that accumulations to the present would doubtless be over $6 billion.
Would the minister say those undistributed profits and depreciation allowances were adequate? I wonder if he would think, with his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), that the profits of the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company were too high. It was only a few days ago that we heard in the house that the profits of the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company were too high. Maybe the Minister of Trade and Commerce should take part in this debate and tell the house if he feels the same when he looks at the profits of, let us say, the Aluminum Company of Canada as he does when he scowls at those of the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company.

do not know they are going to get is not a very bright prospect, or one that is very likely to lighten the burden of the farmers. Our farmers are entitled to much more consideration at a time when farm produce prices are falling. During 1952 the wholesale price index of farm produce fell 19 per cent, while the price of labour was rising by 7 per cent. In the 12 months from November 1951 to November 1952 the new consumer price index fell 1-8 points, but it was due very largely to the fall in farm prices which, in turn, brought food costs lower.
The farmers of Canada have borne practically the entire cost of the year's decline in living costs for the whole of our population. In my judgment that is not fair. That sort of thing has been done too often in the past. Meanwhile the cost of things the farmers will have to buy-machinery, repairs, building materials, fertilizers and all of those things- has shown very little, if any, reduction. It was only natural, therefore, that they should look for some consideration in the budget, and they deserved better treatment either in the budget or under a more realistic trade policy than they were given.
The western federation of agriculture has asked for an increase in trade with Britain; acceptance of sterling in payment for that part of our exports for which the United Kingdom and other members of the sterling bloc cannot pay dollars; a much better and more favourable long-term production credit arrangement; and much more two-way trade. I think all these things are reasonable and just, and certainly they are essential in the interests of a strong band of farmers and a strong Canada. I shall have something to say about trade shortly, perhaps before I have finished this evening.
Just at this point I should like to mention one or two specific things about the budget, particularly the taxes set out therein. What has happened in the field of cigarettes is an example of how this government almost killed the cow that was supplying a good many Canadian families with milk. We on this side of the house warned them of what was going to happen when they jacked up the cigarette tax a couple of years ago. But they would not listen to us; not at all. Now look what they have had to do.
Then the Minister of Finance had some pungent things to say about the nuisance taxes when he announced the removal of the stamp tax. It is interesting to note how easy it becomes for the minister to see clearly, in an election year, that a beloved tax is really a nuisance tax. And I say "beloved" because the minister admitted the other day that the

tnought of abolishing the stamp tax caused him to mourn. I am glad to see the stamp tax go, and I cannot bring myself to shed many tears over it. But I can bring myself to shed tears over the fact that he overlooked the kiddies in the country, and kept on a lot of nuisance taxes that might very well have been taken off: the tax on chocolate bars and on nickel candy, and that sort of thing. But I suppose the kiddies have to be sort of kept in line.
Then I think the minister should have abolished the 4 per cent floor on medical expenses, deductible from income tax. Of course 3 per cent is better than 4 per cent, but for whom? That is the question; for whom? Certainly it is not for the ordinary fellow, because he cannot take advantage of it under any circumstances. I will say the minister ought to have done something worth while for the little fellow by abolishing that 4 per cent floor entirely.
Because I like the minister and have a high personal regard for him I am now going to point out to him some sources of revenue that might be explored with profit both to the treasury and to the country as a whole. It is not often we give the minister ideas, but maybe this will help him. As he doubtless knows, there are quite a number of foreign magazines circulating in this country. Some of them put on a heavy sales pressure for advertising from Canadian business. My opinion is that they have taken a very large slice of advertising revenue away from some of our Canadian dailies and periodicals. Some newspapers in our country are hard hit as a consequence. The minister might consider putting a stiff tax on that kind of advertising in foreign periodicals in order that a healthy Canadian opinion can be maintained by a strictly Canadian press. I feel sure that such a result would be quite in larmony with the Massey report, and it cer-;ainly would be desirable. I pass that on ;o the minister for what it is worth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that I will be unable to justify the generosity of members of this house in this, my first attempt to address you, sir, and through you the people of this country, in a considerable period of time. If I ask the privilege tonight of speaking more particularly of that great country in which I am more interested, it is because of the fact, sir, that I am afraid I am not able to take part in debate as often as I would wish; and I am of the opinion that my time would be better employed, rather than entering into an argument with the hon. gentleman who has just finished his address, to say what I believe ought to be done on behalf of the country where I have lived for over 60 years and on behalf of people I have represented for over 30 years.
Before I proceed further may I say that I will try to deal in these 40 minutes with many things that I have in mind; but I would be derelict in my duty if I did not remind the house of what I suggested regarding the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) after he presented his first budget to this house many years ago. I had taken the opportunity of congratulating the Right Hon.
2370	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Dechene James L. Ilsley on the tremendous work he had done during the war and on what he had accomplished with incredible courage and ability on behalf of this country in its time of peril and danger. I said I was pleased to see that he was being succeeded by one of the most brilliant young men in the political life of Canada that day.
I listened to the minister the other night, and in spite of the things that have been said today and that will be said as the debate goes on I want to say to you, sir, that I belong to the school which believes that you do not abuse a man all his lifetime and then build him a monument after he dies. If you have anything nice to say about a man, tell him now. After listening to his speech the other night I was prouder than ever to be a Canadian and a Liberal.
I do not agree with the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). As other Liberals realize, in spite of the fact that this Korean trouble arose which compels the minister to come before parliament and ask for sums so enormous as to stagger the imagination; in spite of that terrific burden imposed on the country in order to keep our pledges to our allies to keep this world free; in spite of those enormous sums of money required the minister has been able to come before parliament, because of the wisdom of the administration of this government, after reducing the public debt over the last few years by over $2J billion, and tell the people of Canada: Today I am able to reduce your taxes by an amount of over $360 million a year.
Mr. Speaker, there has been an attempt to tell the little man that he has not received anything.
Well, I am a little man. I am not a lawyer, and I am rather pleased about that lately. I am not a teacher. I have been a farmer and a homesteader. Of course you will understand, sir, why I am saying everything that is in my heart. I do not need any notes. Everything I believe, everything I have lived for in order to serve those who have entrusted me with their representation today, I am placing before you in order to deserve their confidence.
This afternoon I listened to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I heard him deplore the fact that the little man was not getting anything from this tough Minister of Finance. At that time I happened to be reading a document he had written and presented to the legislature of Alberta on March 17, 1933, when he was representing the mortgage associations of this country. I was a member of the legislature at that time. He came pleading with us not to interfere with the sacredness of their mortgages. This


happened at a time when the great majority of the farmers of our province, along with the farmers of other western provinces, were in desperate circumstances. The legislature of Alberta thought it necessary to pass some measure of adjustment in order that farmers would not be driven from their land. They could not dispose of their products at fair prices. Under the Tory regime wheat was selling at 25 cents a bushel and hogs were delivered to the market for $1.70.
This hon. member told us that he did not want to hurt the poor farmer. No; all he wanted to do was to keep him in bondage forever. He wanted to keep him on the land and would not bother him until things got better. Then he would keep the farmer in bondage until doomsday. The members of the legislature wanted to pass some measure to enable these men to stay on their land, and to do that they had to cut down the farmer's liability to the point where he could afford to stay there and have a chance of making a comeback. I take the hon. member's complaints today, therefore, this great representative of the poor people, with a grain of salt. This is the official record which I have here. I was a member at that time, so I do not need to rely on hearsay.
Then we had another great series of speeches made to us when social credit was preached to the people of Alberta. We heard that the man who was responsible for this great new orientation of democracy, as Mr. W. Wood liked to say, was a man by the name of Major Douglas. Apparently he never tried this doctrine, except on himself, because it paid him handsomely to talk about it. It was decided to invite this man to attend our legislature and explain social credit to us. He was on his way from New Zealand, where they had turned him down, and was travelling from Vancouver on his way home to England. He was only a few hours away from Edmonton, but do you know how much he wanted before he would attend this meeting? He wanted $2,000, and not in social credit but cold cash, before he would consent to appear before the legislature of Alberta to tell us about this scheme which we did not understand and which nobody understands today.
We do not need experts to explain these schemes to our men, no matter whether they are ordinary labourers with an ordinary education or farmers or anyone else. We do not need an expert to come from overseas to explain any scheme for the government of this country which may be of benefit to the people of this country. The ordinary man is smart enough to understand it, and if it is no good he will turn it down. In this case this gentleman tried it, and is still trying. That

should be sufficient on that score, because we have something more important to talk about.
I know you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, as will the hon. members, to speak about matters that may appear of a local nature to you. Hon. members from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland or Quebec may say that my remarks apply to only a small part of the country, but that is not so. If they will permit me to speak for a few minutes I shall tell them, in a manner they can fully understand, that Athabaska stands in the middle of a new empire which is now in the making. We are at the headwaters of this great fluvial route to the north. There is the Athabasca, as well as many other large rivers-the Peace river, the Pembina, the Smoky, the Wapiti, the Clearwater and others'-with a tremendous flow towards the Arctic ocean for thousands of miles north of Edmonton. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that Hansard is able to follow my humble remarks tonight because I have no prepared copy of this speech. There are those who go around this country taking credit for the discovery of oil in Alberta. In 1932 I submitted a resolution to the Alberta legislature asking the government to help in the exploration for oil which I felt was underneath our soil.
At the time my hon. friend the Minister of Finance made his first budget speech I told him that within a few years he would be able to close out his books without a worry and the balance of trade would be in our favour, all because of the tremendous oil resources that would be discovered in Alberta. It may have been only a hunch. As someone once said, I am an optimist. In any event, the oil was discovered. In my constituency, at the junction of the Clearwater and Athabasca rivers, there is a field of oil so great and so valuable that there is nothing comparable to it in the world; and that is not just talk. Engineers from the United States bureau of mines, from Toronto and other places came to report upon it. Even at the lowest estimate there are over 500 billion barrels of oil in these sands, and that is only what we have seen s6 far.
There are also by-products, such as paving material and everything one can imagine. We import this paving material from Trinidad, and we pay tribute to the large oil companies for the material to pave our roads. At the same time, right in Athabaska, there is enough of this material to pave every street in this Canada of ours.
You may say this is a provincial matter. Well, it is not. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) was quite free with his challenge when he started his address tonight. There may be a challenge for him here to
The Budget-Mr. Dechene look into. During the war one of the finest businessmen ever to serve this country, to the detriment of his health and his business, was the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who was then minister of munitions and supply. He took advantage of the provisions of the War Measures Act to take over the property owned by the Abasand Oils company at Fort McMurray, and enter into the production of this oil.
I wonder if you remember how many times this was criticized in this house. Men have stood up in their places here, members from Alberta, and have criticized it. Instead of boosting it and trying to develop it, instead of taking advantage of the war situation to see that any possible means of separating the oil would be found, and doing everything that they could, they did everything possible to destroy the attempts of this government to develop that great natural wealth in the tar sands.
I remember that in February, 1945, I was astounded to find the propaganda that was going around there. It was heartbreaking propaganda, put out for purely political purposes, to retard the development of that vast resource right in our own country. That was done at a time when tankers were being sunk on the Atlantic coast, as you know, by the German submarines, and when we did not know but that the day might soon come when we would be without this fuel, without which we cannot carry on a war let alone carry on in time of peace. This devolopment was actually and effectively stopped by propaganda, and I found out the reason for it only later.
If anyone is interested, he can go to the city of Edmonton and ask the provincial secretary's department there to show him the deal that was entered into between a department of the provincial government of Alberta and a man who was a promoter all his life, who has made his living without having to work a day. He was given by the provincial government practically control of the entire area of the vast tar sands in that vicinity. I challenge anyone to deny this fact, because I myself saw this document, Mr. Speaker. I happen to have some friends in the city of Edmonton. I speak about a matter that appears to be provincial because we are not doing our duty by this country if we allow foreign companies to get entire control of our natural resources which are so valuable in oil and when we do not open up the incredible wealth of the tar sands in the Athabasca basin.
May I be allowed to have a thought for those who discovered that great Athabasca country. In the centre of the constituency
2372	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Dechene of Athabaska is a place called Lac la Biche which was discovered a long time ago, as time goes in this young country. It was discovered over a century or a century and a half ago. A mission was established there by those hardy pioneers. The missionaries were the ones, with Captain Shot, we called him, because he shot the rapids on the Athabasca. His name was Fosseneuve and his descendants are still in that great country which I represent. He was the first man to discover a route through Lac la Biche, the La Biche river, the Athabasca river and on down to the Arctic ocean, a route which was taken over by the pioneer company and all the great traders of the north country, which had been discovered by those hardy pioneers. That is why Athabaska so greatly appeals to me. That is why I am willing to devote the declining years of an active life to serving this pioneering population.
I have not much time left, Mr. Speaker, but in 1945-

-I want to say that we acted along with the others in this country. We are talking about unity, and I know that most of us are united. May I say, in diverging for a moment, sir, that since coming to Ottawa I have been proud of the men and women I have met from other provinces: those strong, generous men from the provinces by the sea; I refer to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. I have been proud to meet those from central Canada, from my ancestral home, the old province of Quebec to which my ancestors first came in 1632.
I must admit that there is a great deal of narrowness yet, unfortunately, amongst some part of our people. This is the forum, is it not, in which to speak about the matter? Where else can I do so? I will say this on the platform anywhere; but so that the people of the country may hear, so that my message may carry beyond the walls of this building and may carry beyond the boundaries of my constituency, I believe I can quite properly and justifiably take advantage of the forum of this house in pleading this case with you, Mr. Speaker, and with the members of parliament.
In 1945 I was, as you will remember, the only Liberal member elected in Alberta from a rural area. There was one from a city. It just happens that because the people know me well and have confidence in me, the great majority of those of French extraction voted for me in that election, as they did in the past and as they will in the next. It was a close fight, a fight between gentlemen, citizens of Canada, with only one aim and TMr. Dechene.]

one ambition. Although we might differ as to methods by which it may be achieved, our one concern is for the welfare and the happiness of this great country.
May I say that I never heard of a race being insulted as were the French Canadians in that election by the defeated candidate. The language he used cannot be put on Hansard or anywhere else. If a man used it in the street he would be arrested right away. They insulted them, through the mud they tried to throw at this important part of our population. That conduct should deny them the right ever to appeal to that class in Athabaska or elsewhere in the future.
I am not trying to use this as a lever or as something in my favour. We are not by far the majority in that great constituency of Athabaska, but I want to protest against this kind of thing. That is why I mention it on the floor of this house. I am not the only one who heard it. There were many men and women there; and some of his own supporters called me outside and told me he should be ashamed for insulting such an important and pioneering part of our great population in Alberta and in Athabaska. I know the words he used. Don't worry; I shall never forget them. If any man ever utters that same kind of language again and ever appears on a platform, I do not care if I live to be 90 years of age, I shall be delighted to meet him and call him by his proper name.
Now I have something else to talk about and it has been the subject of many a debate in the past. I am sorry to say that so far I have been unable to get any support, for reasons that I ignore, from the present party in authority in the province of Alberta. I am speaking about this great new artery of transportation for which plans were made away back in 1927 and 1928. It is not a local issue. It concerns the four western provinces, and at least three of them vitally, namely northwestern Saskatchewan, the whole of northern Alberta and northern British Columbia. This was provided for by arrangement between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, by which, in order to bring about this development in a country which had a future-which had lakes, forests, mines and everything, besides the best of land-the Canadian National Railways would continue this line from Battleford and St. Walburg to the constituency of Athabaska, and the C.P.R. would come in west of Prince Albert, would have running rights on that line for 55 miles until they reached Cold Lake where the grade was built, and from then the C.N.R. would go down to Edmonton and the C.P.R.
2373 S

would go north of the Beaver river to the Athabasca river and the Peace river, to join with the Northern Alberta Railways at Lac la Biche in Athabaska and join with the Northern Alberta Railways line serving Peace river in order to have an outlet for the western provinces to the Pacific coast.
This is not a new plan, Mr. Speaker. The time has arrived, I believe, when we should talk about this matter. I have spoken about it often. I have been a long time in public life and I have found out that you must keep going after these things. You must speak about them. You must agitate. You must seek the support of your fellow members. You must seek the support of the government. It will not be done in a day, I know. I do not expect it to be done tomorrow. But unless we push and press for it, it will not be done at all.
If the Korean war terminates, and if Uncle Joe behaves himself, then this country will be in a position to carry on with the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways for the construction of this great outlet. The other day it was mentioned by the new premier of British Columbia, who by the way was a strong Conservative until a few weeks before the election and who used to live in Athabaska. All kinds of people live there. Mr. Bennett used to be a citizen of our country.

speechtext:
We chased him out; we gave him to you. As I was saying, the premiers of Alberta and British Columbia met together and amongst other propositions they suggested a western outlet through one pass which is not the one that should be used anyway, but they suggested it. They entirely forgot, Mr. Speaker, that no government will ever build a railway which would cost $125 million to $150 million just for the purpose of developing that part of northern Alberta west of Lesser Slave lake. In order to ensure the success of such an undertaking there are only a few gaps to close between Battleford and Prince Albert in Saskatchewan to my country of Athabaska, and the city of Edmonton and this Peace river country. There are just a few short gaps to fill in to provide a line right through to the northern half of these great provinces with every possible resource, all the best of land, wheat and pasture land, cattle country, fish abounding, great lakes and timber resources of all kinds. These resources should all be linked together. In order for this project to succeed they would have to join with these others that I have been speaking about for so long and that I have been pleading
The Budget-Mr. Dechene for, so that whole empire a thousand miles wide will be served by this Peace river outlet.
I had a few notes here but I seem to have mislaid them. I do not want to refer to a previous debate, Mr. Speaker, following your ruling; but I must say that I was astounded at the attitude of the opposition.
It was not the budget that was being discussed at all. The attitude of the opposition was that there would be an election and they had nothing against this government; how could they? It is the same old tactics that were used in 1911 and again in 1917.

speechtext:
I have pleaded this for years. I will put it this way. A woman whom I have known since she was a little child, who is married and has a large family living, and who is raising them well through hard work, wrote to me. She believes in the nobility of work. She and her husband do not want anything for nothing. They want to earn the bread they eat. She wrote to me and said: "Mr. Dechene, how is it that they are drilling on my land? There is gas and oil under my land." A refinery was built and opened there in my home town, and I had the honour to be invited when it was opened. She said: "How is it that these men can walk on my land and just give me a little bit for the surface rights?
If I do not agree they go to arbitration, and they say, well, it is worth $100 an acre, or so; yet I have all that value under my feet. There are millions of dollars worth of gas and oil under my feet." They have devoted so much work to the land. She said: "I have seen my husband almost fainting from hard work taking the trees and stones out by the sweat of his brow, and there is a well under our feet and I have no title to it whatever, not one cent." They go before this democratic government, which says that this is an expendable resource. It actually is, of course. And they say they are going to use it in a revolving fund to finance the municipalities and the school districts.


This may not be of interest to you, but there is a point here and I have spoken on it very often. This is a plan under which they will keep the municipalities and the school districts in bondage to the government forever and ever, and they will have to pay interest on it; and they will never be out from under the direct control of these people. I protest again that this is the only forum before which I can bring the views of the people concerned.
Now, I said a moment ago that, in spite of the conditions created by the unfortunate Korean development, in spite of rearmament, in spite of doing our share in NATO, spending all those millions of dollars in a time of peace, we have succeeded in keeping the ship of state sailing on smooth waters, and in keeping the people of this country content and prosperous.
I remember, sir, saying at one time to some young members who were listening to me in this house-and I must say that I gave them some advice-to never hesitate to carry on with something in which they believed. I advised them never to let anything stand in their way, that they should not be discouraged if they did not succeed at first. Because, as I pointed out to them, things are not done that way. I said to them that if they thought they were right they should carry on, that they should have confidence in the cause they espoused. Carry on, and some day they would be surprised that what they have advocated had been accomplished.
That is all we can do in these times. And, just as I gave encouragement to those young men, I would give it to the present members of the House of Commons, speaking always in my humble capacity as a private member. Sir, there is no more beautiful land under the sun of God than Alberta in June. You know, our flower in Alberta is the wild rose. And I do not think finer will be found anywhere, even in the Rocky mountain area or anywhere else, not even excluding the Niagara peninsula. I was over in the St. Catharines area, a paradise in the spring; but I do not think I saw anything as beautiful as the prairies blooming in the sun in June, as we see it in northern Alberta. There is no night there; it is daylight almost all the time.
And the flowers, sir, the roses; tall as trees, and scattered throughout the land. Marvellous; simply marvellous. Beautiful. It creates a new heart in life, a gratitude to this merciful God who, after all the dictators, is still boss. In Alberta in June-and some day, when the Lord is ready, as we say in French, les desseins du Seigneur sont insondables- they are too deep for us.

And may I say to some of my good friends across the way just this: The other day one of them, the juvenile member for Kamloops, was objecting to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) being out of the chamber- the Prime Minister who is carrying such a burden, who has to look after all these responsibilities of government in onerous times. But because he left the house on other business he was criticized. I was going to say to those young fellows something in French-and I hope there is a French shorthand writer in the house-something in all humility, which I recite myself, so that it may be realized that I am just a humble servant of the Almighty:
Acte d'humilite: Mon Dieu, je ne suis que cendre et poussiere reprimez les mouvements d'orgueil qui s'elevent dans mon ame, et apprenez-moi a me mepriser moi-meme, 6h Vous qui resistez aux su-perbes et donnez votre grace aux humbles.
Mr. Speaker, the autocrats of this day will disappear, just as the great autocrats and warriors of the past have disappeared. God will remain. It is in Him we trust. You may have noticed,. Mr. Speaker, that I make it a point to be in the chamber when prayers are recited each day, because they are such fine prayers, and you recite them so well. It is moving, indeed. And God will be in His heaven when the memory of those great warriors will have disappeared into the dust of the centuries. If at times it seems to take long for things we desire to happen we must remember this, that on God's eternal clock the centuries are but the minute hand. And just as the farmer when he sows his land in the spring, after spending a lot of money and backbreaking labour, has to wait upon God's will for the beneficent rain and sunshine, and lifts his anxious eyes to heaven, let us in this House of Commons do the same thing.
My last word is a very humble word of confidence in this country, its valiant people and, I will add, and without any hesitation, confidence in this government.
