subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with those of my class, that is the working class, I regret that the budget presented to this house last Thursday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) does not provide for greater income tax reductions in so far as the small wage earner is concerned, and that no change has been made in the method of levying taxes on farmers who carry on family farming, which is the kind of farming done on most farms in the province of Quebec.
The Budget-Mr. Spence
In view of the high cost of living, the budget just laid before the house by the Minister of Finance would indeed have been better received, and it would above all have answered a need which the representatives of the working class have been voicing for a long time, if it had provided for reductions and rates more in keeping with the demands of labour. The new tax rates are a real disappointment to the working class.
Considering the disclosures made in this house and in the press in connection with the extravagances, the waste, and the thefts committed in the administration of the Department of National Defence, the workers were entitled to hope that, at long last, the government would see fit to act in order to effect economies and control expenditures in that department, so as to reduce the volume of such expenditures to the benefit of the working class, which is constantly being asked to make sacrifices that are considered, not without reason, in view of the recent disclosures of the Currie inquiry, somewhat exaggerated.
The workers are under the impression that they are being fooled for they now have been given the proof that a large portion of the income tax deducted from their pay envelope is being ill-spent, without sufficient control and even, in some cases, without the consent of the responsible authorities.
The workers have never refused to contribute to the administration or to the common effort of national defence; but they are not unaware of the fact that their contribution has, so far, been rather important, through various direct and indirect taxes. As a matter of fact, while the cost of living has been increasing for the past six or seven years, their contribution has grown in proportion to this increase.
The new scale of income tax provides only for an insignificant reduction with regard to small wage earners. I may add that it even penalizes people with dependents as, according to the table published by the hon. the Minister of Finance, a single person earning $2,500 a year will benefit to the extent of $15 for the current year and of $30 for a whole year, while for the head of a family with two dependent children, who earns the same amount, the reduction will only be $2 for the current year-against $15 for a single person-and $4 for a whole year-against $30 for a single person. The single person with an income of $5,000
2376	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Spence will get a reduction of $100 for a whole year, while the head of a family of two children will get a reduction of $39 less than the single person's. And the higher the income, the greater the difference. Independent newspapers have also acknowledged the fact. May I be permitted to quote from an item I read in Le Droit of today just before coming into the house. It is entitled:
"A social dividend unfairly distributed": Mr. Abbott has deemed it advisable to make concessions to every group that complained to him last year. Too bad for those who neglected to do so or who could not find good spokesmen to fight their1 case.
We must say however that the great but indistinct outcry of the people has not been heard as it should have been. Is it because the man in the street is usually ill-prepared to criticize such and such a point of our taxation system? Is it because the humble, the rank and file, do not clearly realize what is wrong about tax reductions? We cannot say. But it is the duty of independent newspapers who have no electoral axe to grind to speak on behalf of the forgotten classes and to enlighten the Minister of Finance on the most serious deficiencies of his last budget.
There is nobody in Canada who does not rejoice that the taxes will be reduced by $250 million for 1953-54. There is nobody also who is not happy that he no longer will have to pay certain nuisance taxes: excise stamps on cheques and money orders, radio licences, etc. But what is the exact amount represented by these two reductions for the average Canadian? Some $5 a year at the very most. The* taxpayers will pay $17 million less in taxes on cigarettes. But then again, the poorest, those who ''rolled? their own, will benefit very little. Those who will profit from it are the manufacturers and the Canadians who can spare 35 or 70 cents a day for 'smokes. As for the $15 million which the public treasury will lose in excise and sales taxes on books, food, etc., the ordinary man's share of this official ''gift" will also be rather small.
Now if under the heading of personal income tax, the individual taxpayers are to be left $87 million more, we must not forget that tax relief is carried out under a rigid mathematical formula, so that if we refer to the very tables submitted by the Minister of Finance, we see that the very simple result of all this is that those who have the greatest load to carry and the least money benefit from no special treatment whatever . . .
It may be stated, without injustice to anyone, that the world of business has been treated more generously- by the Minister of Finance than the average taxpayer. The gross exemptions, under the heading of income tax, will be $87 million for the private individual and $85 million for corporations, for the next fiscal year. Apart from the provision concerning medical expenses, which tends to favour those in the low income brackets, the other cuts will be felt mostly in the higher income groups. The $400 exemption per child attending university,1 though socially equitable, will only favour a minority, and not the poorest. The 20


per cent credit on taxable dividends directly affects businessmen. Business circles will benefit in the proportion of two to one from the abolition of taxes on cheques and negotiable instruments.
It is to be noted that serious reservations must be made with regard to the social effect of the income tax reductions announced last Thursday. It is clear that the advisers to the Minister of Finance have a theoretical conception of the taxpayer. It seems that they have lost all contact with reality, that is the toil and sweat of the humble people. Otherwise, Mr. Abbott's budget would have been different. It would not have shown that mathematical rigidity which is its distinguishing characteristic, nor this tendency to put on an equal footing the worries of the businessman and the misery of the humble people. It would have granted the famous "social dividend", of which the minister spoke, to a greater proportion of those who, socially, are more to be pitied.
The Minister of Finance has missed a wonderful opportunity of earning some rights to the gratefulness of our low income citizens when he failed to grant what our labour organizations and various other associations have so often asked for in the past few years, the raising of the income tax exemptions to $1,500 for single persons, and $3,000 for married people.
The labour group is the hardest hit by taxes. I would even add that it cannot possibly evade it in any way. Unfortunately, it is for this group that the present budget shows the least consideration.
In a speech I made in this house, I appealed to the Minister of National Revenue to rectify an anomaly which exists in our Income Tax Act with regard to family farming, as it is practised in the province of Quebec.
Here is what I said, as may be seen in the translation on page 487 of the English edition of Hansard for December 9, 1952:
I quote the text relating to the matter of family help, In our Income Tax Act, according to the "Farmers and Fishermen Guide'' 1951 edition, as reproduced in the Action Catholique of November 27.
Salaries earned by children are deductible only inasmuch as:
(a)	those salaries have been paid in cash during the year;
(b)	the services were rendered with a view to producing the income;
(c)	the services would otherwise have required the hiring of help; and
(d)	the amount is reasonable, taking into account the child's age and the wages which would otherwise be paid to an outside worker to perform the same task.
One cannot claim as expenses the value of the upkeep of dependent children.
The Action Catholique from which the quotation is drawn goes on to say:
Let us assume that a farmer has three sons and that the work they do on the land is not paid for, for this land will one day be theirs and they shall

profit by the improvements to it. Now if, in this case, the father does not pay his children any wages, all the income from the soil will be considered from the point of view of income tax, as having been earned by only one man, that is by the head of the family. This situation is unfair and contrary to common sense, but it nevertheless exists under our present Income Tax Act.
The present act considers only the case where the wages in question have been paid during the current year, so that wages earned during preceding years cannot be considered in such cases when for example death comes to the head of the family, and they can be deducted only if they have been used to pay for services designed to produce revenues and for which the farmer would otherwise have had to hire help.
Such a principle, when applied, means that farmers who pay wages to the members of their family cannot enter those wages in their expense accounts since in a great many cases the farmers would not have hired extra help to do the work.
The representatives of our farmers have kept up their plea for amendments to the Income Tax Act.
For instance, UAction Catholique, on February 19 last, published the following:
In the great majority of cases, agriculture in Quebec greatly differs from that of other parts of Canada, of western Canada for instance. In those districts agriculture is organized on a business basis, while ours is a family organization. The present Income Tax Act is well suited for commercialized agriculture but is badly fitted to our needs.
In our province, through a family spirit which honours us, farmers group together to make a success of their agricultural venture. Sometimes we see young children do work too strenuous for them, but this barely permits making a small financial success of the enterprise.
But the Department of National Revenue refuses to recognize the fact that although the income is all in the name of the father, a good part of it rightly comes to his children. The father could surely pay them a salary in the form of a loan and get the money back afterwards: this would enable the children to gradually become owners of the farm. But very few fathers are conversant with these provisions of the law and put them into practice in a fair and reasonable way.
Very often a farmer owns property valued at, say, $10,000 to $15,000, on which taxation officials are seeking to collect income tax, when in fact such property is the result of the courage and sacrifices of the whole family.
It is amazing, Mr. Speaker, that this government, though they received from Quebec, if I am not mistaken, quite a substantial measure of support at the last election, has not deemed it advisable to implement these requests put forward by our farmers and our salaried people.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to draw the attention of the house to the fact that, despite these seemingly prosperous times, there are at present, in our district of Saguenay-Lake St. John, more than 6,500 wage earners drawing unemployment benefits. If we add to this number those who are not receiving this assistance, we easily reach a total exceeding
10,000	unemployed.
68108-152i
The Budget-Mr. Spence
Lumbering operations, which provide our farmers with an important source of revenue, especially when farm products sell badly, such as has been the case for more than a year, have been greatly reduced this year.
The lumber camps, which are generally active until March, ceased operating early in December, and have not employed half the number of people they have been employing over the past few years. Our farmers were the first to be affected by these layoffs.
On the other hand, in the past three years, two very important electric power stations have been erected on the Peribonca river, one at the Chute du Diable and the other at the Chute a la Savanne. Now these two stations gave work, while construction was going on, to close to 5,000 men. They have now been completed and those 5,000 men, a large majority of whom live in the towns and villages of my constituency and of the neighbouring constituency of Lake St. John, are now without employment.
I deem it my duty to draw the attention of the house to the critical situation which is the. lot of a great number of farmers and workers of my district on account of that unemployment and I venture to make a suggestion which, if implemented at once, would greatly help alleviate this crisis.
The cost of living being as high as it is now, and incomes being such that it is not possible to make both ends meet, when the head of a family becomes unemployed, the greatest misery follows.
Some 140 miles northwest of my county, there is a rich mining area, which we call the Chibougamau district.
According to the information I have, there are in that district, where the first prospecting operations were started more than 80 years ago, more than 225 companies owning land, and everything indicates that there is hope that these mining developments will be a success.
There can be no more doubt about the wealth and abundance of those deposits; the price of metals today is sufficiently high to permit profitable development. A market would be ensured for those metals. Hydroelectric power is relatively easy to obtain. A magnificent highway already makes it easier to get there by truck and automobile and to ensure the success of the development we only need a railroad.
Mining operations are already under way and according to the Progres du Saguenay of November 13, 1952, the Campbell Chibougamau Mines Limited have already obtained a contract from the U.S. government defence materials procurement agency for 63,200,000
2378	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Spence pounds of copper and for all the cobalt that can be produced, at 24| cents a pound. The delivery date has even been set and delivery must be made before December 31, 1956.
A modem city is being erected there, including a church, a school and public buildings. In the spring more than 500 technicians will be employed by some four or five companies that have started or will soon start operations on their deposits and in 1954 that number will be doubled.
No less than eight air transport companies are needed to take technicians in and out. In all assurance, I can say to the house that at least $40 to $50 million have been spent in our district, in the last fifty years, towards its development. However, transport difficulties have always made prospecting and drilling operations extremely costly and even from 1929 to 1948, the airplanes were the only means of transport. Before 1929, the Chibougamau district could only be reached by water or by dog sled. These difficulties have not deterred courageous and enterprising men from working perseveringly in order to show how rich this mining district is; in fact, in some cases, they put all their money in it.
The opening of a highway, three or four years ago, gave much stimulus to the development of the mining deposits. This road had made it possible to transport the necessary heavy machinery and will make it possible to take out the ore until the railway has been built.
Private enterprise has not been backward in spending money. The Quebec government has generously contributed close to $6 million for road construction. In my opinion then, and in the opinion of everybody who lives in that district, it would be high time for the federal government to play its part in this undertaking by enabling the Canadian National Railways to construct a line by which the ore could be hauled from the Chibougamau district as economically as possible.
We learn through the newspapers that a delegation from the council for economic guidance of the Saguenay-Lake St. John district will soon call upon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). They will present a memorandum, carefully prepared by eminent economists, on the economic advantages which would accrue from the construction of such a railroad. It is therefore useless to acquaint the house with them.
Nevertheless, I thought I should talk about this matter, since the line which is requested will start from the constituency I represent


here and also because I am very interested in seeing that as early a start as possible be made towards the implementation of that project.
Since I was not invited to participate in the drafting of the memorandum which will be submitted to the Minister of Transport, and since I shall not be able to join the delegation on March 2 next, I would not like to have the people of my county think that, if I am not a member of the delegation, it is because I am not in favour of this railway project.
As a matter of fact, I believe that even if this railway were to have a deficit at the start, it should still be built. We have built railways which, after twenty years of operation, have not yet succeeded in balancing their budget.
As the Canadian National Railways is a state enterprise, even if our railway in Chibougamau shows a slight deficit at the start, the government will be largely compensated by the revenues which it will receive from other sources as a result of the new developments that this new railway will undoubtedly bring about.
In my opinion, when the state considers the soundness of a project it must not only consider the immediate benefits to be derived therefrom.
When we spend billions of dollars for national defence, we certainly do not expect to derive any financial benefits therefrom. These billions are the price we have to pay for our freedom and our way of life.
Therefore if the government votes a sum of $16 or $17 million for the construction of this new proposed railway, it will provide employment, increase the national wealth, ensure the economic stability of the area, the development of which will thus be made possible, and will, in return, derive very interesting direct and indirect revenues in the form of various taxes.
One might object perhaps that we do not have the necessary money to carry out such a project. My answer to that would be that the necessary funds might easily be obtained if a stricter control were exercised on the expenditure of money appropriated for national defence.
The few instances of waste that we have been able to find in this field give us reason to doubt the validity of an argument of that kind.

The question is of great importance to the economic stability of the Saguenay-Lake St. John district.
To bring this speech to its conclusion, I shall remind the government that in the past they have never bestowed their favours upon our district and especially upon my county, in such a way as to spoil us. It would therefore be a convenient opportunity for the present government to make amends for the complete oblivion, we might say, in which they have kept us.
The Budget-Mr. Spence
